title: ‘Incredibly encouraging’: healing the scars of traditional anchors in Dorset’s seagrass meadows
content: Eco-moorings help to restore seagrass in just five years, boosting sealife such as seahorses, eels and crabsOne of the UK’s most precious underwater habitats – Dorset’s seagrass meadows – is recovering thanks to “eco moorings” designed to prevent the seabed being ripped up, a study has revealed.Scars caused by traditional anchors in some areas of seagrass in Studland Bay have almost entirely vanished, which is boosting the number of seahorses that thrive in the submerged meadows. title: ANDAPA - L’épargne et le crédit se construisent en communauté
content: Une tenue commune pour renforcer l’esprit d’association et l’unité des membres.Une caisse, trois clés et une règle simple : l’argent mis de côté doit servir à avancer. À Andapa, 228 Voamami, ou associations villageoises d’épargne et de crédit, réunissent des ménages autour de ce principe. La caisse la plus importante atteint 28,94 millions d’ariary. Derrière cette somme, une pratique s’installe : épargner ensemble pour pouvoir investir lorsque l’occasion se présente. Intégré à l’Asa Avotra Mirindra, programme de filets sociaux productifs, le Voamami permet aux membres d’obtenir de petits crédits pour financer leurs projets, notamment leurs activités génératrices de revenus. Chaque membre contribue notamment à hauteur de 500 ariary par semaine pour l’épargne sociale. Des parts peuvent également être achetées à 2 000 ariary l’unité, selon les règles de l’association.Le bénéfice est concret pour ceux qui utilisent le crédit pour faire tourner leur activité. Une participante spécialisée dans la vente de friperie a ainsi pu acheter deux balles de friperie grâce à son emprunt. « L’argent du Voamami porte ses fruits lorsqu’il est réellement utilisé pour le projet prévu », explique Julie Annie, agent villageoise, en rapportant son expérience. Le prêt n’est toutefois qu’une partie du système. La véritable particularité du Voamami se trouve dans sa culture. Ici, la confiance se construit au fil des réunions. Il n’y a pas de compte bancaire : l’argent est conservé dans une caisse dont trois clés sont détenues par trois membres différents. Les opérations se déroulent devant le groupe. Chacun sait ce qui entre, ce qui sort et dans quel cadre l’argent est utilisé.Cette organisation impose aussi une discipline. Les retards et les absences aux réunions peuvent être sanctionnés selon le règlement établi par l’association. Les membres apprennent ainsi à respecter les engagements pris collectivement. La confidentialité des informations sur les épargnes et les crédits renforce également la confiance. Le crédit est remboursé sur trois mois, avec un intérêt de 10 %. Ces intérêts restent dans la caisse et permettent au capital de progresser. Au terme du cycle de neuf mois, le capital et les intérêts sont répartis entre les membres selon leur niveau d’épargne.Plus qu’une simple caisse, le Voamami crée ainsi une petite économie à l’échelle de la communauté: on épargne ensemble, on se fait confiance, on investit et on fait fructifier collectivement l’argent.Fanilo Mampianintsoa

title: Netherlands sets out route map to phase out fossil fuels
content:
Netherlands sets out route map to phase out fossil fuels

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on GoogleThe Netherlands has become the second country in the world to publish detailed plans of how it intends to end its dependence on fossil fuels.
The Dutch government followed France in outlining a so-called “route map” to phasing out oil, gas and coal, in the run-up to the UN Climate Change Conference in Turkey in November.
The plan drew praise from international climate change experts for giving definition to the Netherlands’ ambitions, but there was also criticism for the failure to set a firm deadline.
The decision to draw up national route maps was an outcome of a smaller-scale summit organised by the Netherlands and Colombia in April to discuss moving away from fossil fuels, which 50 countries attended.
France was the first country to publish its plan, which was mostly a summary of existing policies and targets, such as ending the use of coal by 2030, oil by 2045 and gas by 2050.
The Dutch plan includes a reassertion of its commitment to stop using coal-fired power stations to produce electricity by 2030, but other targets have been delayed or downgraded.
Goals downgraded
The Netherlands has reduced the amount of wind energy it wants to produce at sea, abandoned its goal of making the electricity network CO2 free by 2035 and will not meet the EU’s target of reducing emissions by 90% by 2040.
Natalie Jones, of the International Institute for Sustainable Development, said the Dutch plan was a “good example for other countries”.
But climate campaigners were more critical. Maarten de Zeeuw of Greenpeace Nederland told Trouw: “The biggest problem is that unlike France, there is no clear end date. You can call it a route map, but you don’t know where the route is going.”
Joyeeta Gupta, professor of environment and development at the University of Amsterdam, said the plan did not go far enough, given that the limit for global warming of 1.5 degrees C, set in the 2015 Paris Agreement, has almost been reached.
“Already 25 million people a year are fleeing because of the climate crisis, and that is just one of the many terrible consequences,” she said.
A spokesman for the Dutch environment ministry said the route map reflected the Netherlands’ ambition to lead the group of countries that wanted to take a pro-active role on climate change. “The fact that we have made our own route map helps our credibility,” the spokesman said.

title: Chien qui aboie, hibou qui hulule… Mais quel est le cri du renard ?
content:
On pense souvent connaître le renard, ce canidé sauvage discret et rusé qui peuple nos forêts comme nos périphéries urbaines. Pourtant, une question très simple continue de prendre de court les passionnés de nature : quel est le nom exact de son cri ? Contrairement au chien qui aboie ou au hibou qui hulule, le cri du renard ne possède aucun terme unique dédié dans la langue française. On parle plutôt de vocalisations, un ensemble sonore complexe comprenant glapissements, hurlements, jappements et couinements. Longtemps méconnu du grand public, ce répertoire s’avère pourtant indispensable à la survie de l’animal et à sa cohabitation avec les activités humaines.
Un répertoire vocal d’une précision chirurgicale
Loin d’être un animal silencieux, le renard utilise ses vocalisations pour transmettre des messages précis à ses congénères ou à ses rivaux. Chaque type de son remplit une fonction sociale ou défensive bien ciblée.
Le glapissement constitue la première ligne de défense acoustique. Ce cri bref et particulièrement perçant sert d’alerte face à un danger imminent. Lorsqu’un prédateur ou un intrus s’approche, le renard émet ce signal pour prévenir son groupe tout en signifiant explicitement à la menace qu’elle a été repérée, évitant ainsi un affrontement physique inutile.
Durant la période d’accouplement, le paysage sonore change radicalement. Le mâle recourt alors au hurlement, un chant long et strident destiné à marquer son territoire et à attirer les femelles. Accompagné de postures corporelles expressives, ce cri repousse également les rivaux. Les femelles répondent à ces appels par des gémissements ou des glapissements plus courts, instaurant un véritable dialogue vocal entre les partenaires.
Entre adaptation urbaine et cocon familial
Dans un contexte de cohabitation de plus en plus étroite entre la faune sauvage et les zones urbaines, le renard a su ajuster sa communication. Le jappement, qui ressemble à un petit aboiement, sert de signal de vigilance. Il s’avère crucial pour cet animal qui doit continuellement naviguer entre les dangers liés au trafic humain et les menaces animales.
Au sein du terrier, la communication prend une tournure beaucoup plus intime. Les renardeaux émettent des couinements doux et plaintifs pour exprimer la faim ou l’inconfort. Ces signaux permettent à la mère de localiser précisément ses petits dans les dédales sombres de leur habitat souterrain tout en consolidant la cohésion de la portée.
Des variations acoustiques selon l’espèce et l’habitat
L’impact de l’environnement sur ces vocalisations est frappant et varie fortement selon les espèces de renards :
- Le renard roux (Vulpes vulpes) : très répandu en Europe, il se distingue par ses glapissements stridents et ses hurlements puissants qui traversent aisément les bois.
- Le renard polaire (Vulpes lagopus) : habitant des régions arctiques, il produit des fréquences plus graves pour faciliter la portée du son dans l’air glacial.
- Le fennec (Vulpes zerda) : résidant dans les zones désertiques, il émet des vocalisations très aiguës et rapides, évoquant parfois le chant des oiseaux.
Au-delà des différences génétiques, l’habitat modifie directement le rythme des cris au sein d’une même espèce. En forêt dense, les renards prolongent leurs appels pour compenser l’obstacle végétal. À l’inverse, en ville, ils adoptent des vocalisations plus courtes et espacées afin de ne pas attirer l’attention des résidents humains.
Un enjeu majeur pour la cohabitation future
Comprendre la palette sonore du renard dépasse la simple curiosité biologique. À une époque où l’étalement urbain grignote les espaces naturels, cette grille de lecture devient un outil d’éco-citoyenneté. Identifier ces cris permet de réduire les tensions en milieu urbain et d’adapter notre présence pour ne pas perturber les zones de reproduction.
En apprenant à écouter la nuit, le grand public découvre que le renard ne fait pas que passer sans bruit : il entretient un réseau de communication sophistiqué, preuve d’une intelligence adaptative remarquable face aux transformations de son environnement.

title: A Cross-Lingual Acoustic Disease-Alignment Framework for Respiratory Health Assessment from Spontaneous Speech
content: Spontaneous speech offers a scalable, noninvasive signal for respiratory health assessment, yet interpretable models that generalize across languages remain challenging because disease-related acoustic changes are confounded by language-specific phonetic variation. We present CL-DAF, a Cross-Lingual Disease-Alignment Framework that identifies acoustic dimensions whose disease effects remain consistent across languages. Using 201 English and 75 newly collected Bangla speakers, we construct a common 272-dimensional acoustic representation and quantify disease alignment using signed rank-biserial effects and the Language Invariance Score. We first show that spontaneous Bangla speech separates COPD from controls (AUC 0.85); however, 133 features reverse their disease direction across languages and the full representation transfers poorly (AUC 0.49 from Bangla to English). CL-DAF isolates 26 disease-aligned features that raise AUCs to 0.825 and 0.722 from English to Bangla and Bangla to English, respectively. These findings provide a foundation for multilingual clinical speech models emphasizing pathology over language-dependent variation.

title: Maradi a ses 455 tonnes de fournitures ; reste à les faire parvenir jusqu’au dernier village
content: © Gouvernorat de Maradi Huit jours avant la rentrée du 1er octobre, la région se déclare couverte. Le gouverneur mise désormais sur la vigilance des préfets pour que cahiers et crayons atteignent les écoles les plus éloignées. MARADI, 23 septembre 2026— La région dispose désormais de 455 tonnes de fournitures scolaires, un volume que son gouverneur juge suffisant pour couvrir l’ensemble des besoins de l’année 2026-2027. Le Contrôleur général de police Issoufou Mamane a réceptionné officiellement, mercredi, 360 tonnes livrées par le ministère de l’Éducation nationale ; 95 tonnes conservées de l’an dernier complètent le stock. La cérémonie s’est tenue à la Direction régionale de l’Éducation nationale, de l’Alphabétisation et de la Promotion des Langues (DREN). Autour du gouverneur se tenaient le secrétaire général de la région, AbdoulKarim Mahamadou, son adjoint Maman Lawan Mamane, le directeur régional Amadou Harouna, les cadres du système scolaire et les responsables des forces de défense et de sécurité. Une équation qui tourne à l’avantage de la région Les chiffres avancés par le gouverneur permettent de reconstituer le bilan. Les 360 tonnes reçues correspondent à 85 % des besoins que Maradi avait chiffrés et transmis au ministère. Le manque à combler pesait donc une soixantaine de tonnes ; la réserve de 95 tonnes le dépasse d’une trentaine. Le calcul, pas à pas 360 t ÷ 0,85 ≈ 424 t de besoins exprimés 360 t + 95 t = 455 t disponibles, soit environ 31 t de marge. Estimation de la rédaction, établie à partir des pourcentages et volumes donnés par le gouverneur. Fournitures scolaires : un lot complet pour démarrer l'année Le ministère a répondu à la demande formulée par la région. Le lot se compose surtout de cahiers, d’ensembles géométriques, de stylos à bille, de crayons et de correcteur liquide, autrement dit le nécessaire d’un élève comme d’un enseignant pour bien démarrer. Une réserve héritée de l’an dernier Les 95 tonnes en stock racontent l’histoire d’une première dotation qui avait dépassé la consommation. Selon le gouverneur, l’an dernier, la région avait couvert toute l’année scolaire et mis de côté cet excédent. Il rappelle que l’État nigérien accompagne le monde scolaire depuis 2023 pour alléger la charge des familles et du corps enseignant. Le dernier kilomètre, vrai test de la rentrée Le gouverneur a chargé la direction régionale d’acheminer ces fournitures conformément aux instructions des plus hautes autorités. Son message tient en une idée : chaque cahier doit arriver chez « les vrais destinataires ». Il a annoncé qu’il alerterait les préfets et les administrateurs de villes pour que chacun tienne son rôle, jusque dans les villages les plus reculés. "Rien de ce stock ne doit se retrouver sur les étals des marchés, prévient le gouverneur." — Issoufou Mamane, gouverneur de Maradi La région, a-t-il promis, veillera à ce que ces fournitures, acquises à grands frais, ne fassent pas l’objet d’une revente. Il a aussi remercié le Président de la République, le Premier ministre, les membres du CNSP et le gouvernement pour l’effort consenti. La formation technique dans la tournée Le gouverneur a poursuivi sa journée à la Direction régionale de l’Enseignement et de la Formation techniques et professionnels (DREFTP), où le directeur, Mahamane Manou Mahamane Rabiou, lui a présenté le dispositif mis en place. Passer de l’une à l’autre direction, a-t-il expliqué, montre que l’État n’oublie aucun de ses enfants. Il s’attend à ce que les matières d’œuvre suivent, comme l’an dernier, afin que les apprenants reçoivent une formation adaptée aux besoins du marché. Matières d’œuvre : de quoi parle-t-on ? Ce sont les matériaux consommés pendant les travaux pratiques des filières techniques et professionnelles. Leur arrivée conditionne les cours d’atelier. La rentrée des classes Les classes rouvrent le 1er octobre. D’ici là, la direction régionale doit organiser la répartition, et les préfets relayer la consigne sur le terrain. Le gouverneur a souhaité à toute la communauté scolaire une bonne année et de meilleurs résultats. title: Empath: Tracing Multi-Level Emotion Dynamics in Crisis Counseling Dialogues
content: Emotion dynamics are critical for understanding crisis-support conversations, yet most computational work treats emotion as static utterance-level labels. We introduce EMPATH, a framework for understanding affective dynamics in mental health dialogues across three granularities: turn-level labels, transition probabilities, and global conversation archetypes. Applying EMPATH to text-based crisis conversations with self-identified Black texters discussing grief, we find persistent negative affect, gradual hope-ward transitions, distinct texter-volunteer emotional roles, and heterogeneous recovery trajectories. These results highlight the informative patterns that emerge from computationally understanding crisis support and expressions of grief as dynamic processes within conversations, as well as the overall value of emotion-dynamic analysis for analyzing and comparing affect in dialogues.

title: Crested Ibises Released to Help Restore Wild Range
content:
“Twenty crested ibises were released into the wild in Xiaolong Mountain, Tianshui city, Gansu province, on Sunday. This marks a new stage in the province's efforts to restore wild populations of the endangered bird, according to the National Forestry and Grassland Administration.
These crested ibises underwent strict rewilding training and health checks before being fitted with identification tags and released. The move is expected to help the species return to its historical distribution areas, expand its survival space in the wild, and improve the regional conservation network, the administration stated in a media release.
In 1981, only seven wild individuals of the bird were discovered in Yangxian county, Shaanxi province, believed to be the last of their kind. Thanks to over four decades of dedicated conservation, the global population of the crested ibis has now surpassed 10,000, with most residing in Yangxian.”

title: Tarakihi catch limits reduce to 10 per person nationwide
content:
Fisheries Minister Shane Jones says tarakihi catch limits will be reduced, with a nationwide recreational fishing limit of 10 per person.
Commercial limits for the eastern fishery are being reduced by 20 percent, and the western fishery by 55 percent.
Jones said he has considered the latest science and catch information, uncertainty about future stocks of young fish, and the effects of use of the fishery in making the decision.
"These measures will immediately reduce fishing pressure on these tarakihi stocks and put them on more positive trajectories, while allowing a lower level of fishing to continue.
Limits have been increased for snapper and trevally on the North Island's east coast, leatherjacket on the South Island's east and south coast, and frostfish and blue mackerel in deep water.
Butterfish catch limits have also been reduced, with a five-per-person recreational limit.
Seafood NZ chief executive Lisa Futschek said the quota management system was working as intended.
"This process matters. Sustainable fisheries management isn't about catch limits remaining static; it is about making changes when the evidence shows they are needed."
The company's general manager for inshore fisheries Tiff Bock said they supported decisions to ensure tarakihi stocks continued to rebuild.
"Industry has been actively rebuilding east coast tarakihi since 2018 through catch reductions, avoidance measures, gear changes, improved monitoring and significant investment in research. We remain committed to rebuilding the stocks."
Reduction 'does not cut it'
Benn Winlove, a spokesperson for the LegaSea non-profit marine life advocacy group, said a 20 percent reduction on the east coast "does not cut it" and the government should expect further court cases.
"We have watched the stock fall dramatically, with little intervention from officials or successive fishery ministers. Court cases by Forest and Bird and the Environmental Law Initiative have made the government make bigger reductions, but it's not working.
"On the east coast, tarakihi is at 7.7 percent of its estimated original biomass. This is well below the 10 percent hard limit where closure is an option, and the rebuild plan is clearly not working."
The Environmental Defence Society (EDS) said tarakihi fared better on the West Coast at 29 percent of its unfished biomass - but it was in rapid decline.
Policy director Raewyn Peart said EDS sought a total closure of the fishery, until the stocks recovered. Seafood New Zealand and other commercial fishing interests sought the 20 percent reduction in the harvest that was adopted by the minister.
"Given how depleted tarakihi stocks are, and how important this fish is for New Zealanders, the minister's decision is extremely disappointing," said Peart.
"EDS called for a complete closure of the fishery given its perilous state. But the minister's decision doesn't even mention closure as an option. This is despite the eastern stock being below the hard limit, which is when closure needs to be considered under the Harvest Strategy Standard," she said.
Fisheries New Zealand's analysis indicated that the harvest reductions adopted by the minister would mean the stocks would continue to be overfished, Peart said.
"It is also clear the western stock will continue to decline and the eastern stock will remain at very low biomass levels for an extended period. This brings the risk that any adverse event, such as a marine heatwave, could tip it over the edge so it never recovers."
"EDS is now investigating legal options to challenge the decision," Peart said.

title: Can Nepal protect Yomari?
content:
Culture & Lifestyle
Can Nepal protect Yomari?
Why does the country have no legal claim to its own most valuable heritage, and what will it take to build one.Sabina Acharya
Every year, as the month of November-December arrives, the sweet fragrance of steamed rice flour and warm chaku or khuwa fill drifts through the narrow lanes of Bhaktapur, Kathmandu and Lalitpur.
Newa families come together to form small fish-shaped dumplings, known as Yomari, from freshly harvested rice, filled with sesame seeds, coconuts, chaku or khuwa, prepared in a ritual that dates back centuries.
The festival for this food, called Yomari Punhi, is not just a cultural celebration; it is the embodiment of an agricultural knowledge system, linking a particular community, a particular crop, and a particular season.
However, if any foreign food company started producing Yomari today and began labeling it in a supermarket in another country, Nepal would have no legal means to prevent it, as there is no law, no registry, and no enforcement mechanism.
Nepal has 59 officially recognised indigenous nationalities called Adivasi Janajati, comprising around 35 percent of the total population. These span all the ecological zones.
Every community has its own identity, not only in its language and clothing but also in the way it grows its food, prepares its meals, weaves, carves, and heals. Their identity is inseparable from their products.
And yet, while Nepal has precise data on the number of its indigenous communities, it has almost no systematic data on what those communities actually produce.
There is no comprehensive national registry of traditional foods, no catalogue of indigenous medicinal herbs and their community custodians, and no documented inventory of craft techniques and their geographic distribution. Nepal knows it has 59 indigenous nationalities, but it does not know, in any legally useful sense, what those nationalities make, how they make it, or what makes it irreplaceable. A country cannot protect what it has not documented.
Researchers and institutions have identified over 100 agricultural products and 87 potential products that would qualify for international protection as Geographical Indications, a form of intellectual property that protects products whose quality or reputation is tied to a specific geographic origin.
But identification is not documentation. Information about Ilam Tea does not carry the same value as having a legally binding record of its growing altitude, the soil’s characteristics that affect its muscatel taste, and the traditional tea-making processes of the communities who grow it in Ilam. That documentation is required for registration.
For example, compare Yomari with Rasgulla, a centerpiece of one of India’s most famous Geographical Indication disputes, the syrup-soaked cottage cheese ball. The origin of Rasgulla has been disputed for years between West Bengal and Odisha. In 2017, West Bengal was awarded the Geographical Indications status for Banglar Rosogolla, and in 2019, Odisha was awarded the status of GI for Odisha Rasgola, acknowledging the two as separate products from different traditions. Each state’s producers were legally recognised, allowing them to mark their products as authentic, prevent imitations, and establish a market identity tied to their provenance.
Yomari is Nepal’s Rasgulla.
It has a specific community origin, a geographic tie, a centuries-old preparation tradition, and an international diaspora market that already recognises and values it. The difference is that West Bengal and Odisha had a legal system in which to file their claims. Nepal does not.
The same logic applies across Nepal’s entire indigenous product landscape, like Juju Dhau, the King of Yogurt, made in Bhaktapur.
Jumli Marshi rice is grown in Jumla, at an altitude of 2,000-2,900 metres, and depends on the unique flavour and nutritional characteristics of the extreme temperature variations and soil conditions provided by the Karnali region to make it the world’s tallest rice. The weaving density and pattern combinations of Palpali Dhaka fabric are linked to the weaving knowledge tradition practiced by the artisans of Palpa.
Khukuri knives, made by the blacksmith communities in Bhojpur, are known worldwide as a symbol of Nepali craftsmanship due to their curved shape and the steel tempering they undergo. Sherpa, Tamang, and Tibetan Buddhist communities use mineral pigments in a hand-ground technique and iconometric precision to create thangka paintings that are available in international art markets at prices that reflect centuries of value. All these products are potential GI products but are not registered due to the absence of law.
Geographical Indication is the most appropriate legal tool for addressing this. Unlike a patent, it does not require novelty, nor does it require individual authorship as copyright does, nor can it be sold away from the community that owns it, as with a trademark. A GI belongs to all qualified producers in a defined geographic area who meet the production standards.
It is the only form of intellectual property designed for knowledge that is communal, intergenerational, and geographically rooted. And it is the only instrument that connects indigenous communities directly to international markets based on authenticated origin.
The market argument is not abstract. Across international commodity markets, GI-registered products consistently command price premiums over comparable non-registered alternatives. Darjeeling Tea, India’s first GI registration in 2004, commands a price of five to twelve times that of generic Indian black tea in European and Japanese specialty markets.
The Tea Board of India has registered the Darjeeling certification mark in roughly 30 countries. Ilam Tea, grown in ecologically comparable conditions sixty kilometers across the border, is exported to the same markets at a fraction of the price because Nepal has no equivalent certification system.
The farmers of Ilam are not producing an inferior product. They are producing an uncertified one. Nepal’s National Pashmina Sector Export Strategy aims to achieve an export volume of USD75 million in Pashmina by 2026, up from USD15 million in 2023-24.
The goal cannot be accomplished by marketing alone, once the term ‘Pashmina’ has become a generic name for machine-spun blended fiber available in airport stores in Asia and Europe. The only instrument that can restore the word to its authentic meaning and protect that meaning in law is GI registration backed by active enforcement.
This is why the Industrial Property Bill, 2082, introduced to the House of Representatives by the Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies, represents the most significant step Nepal has taken on this issue in its legislative history.
For the first time, the Bill formally recognises Geographical Indications as a distinct and independent category of intellectual property, separated from trademarks, patents, and copyrights. It defines a geographical indication as a sign or geographical name that identifies goods originating from a particular region, where a specific quality, reputation, or characteristic is essentially attributable to that geographical origin.
That definition aligns Nepal, for the first time, with the international standard set by the TRIPS Agreement and with the domestic frameworks of countries that have used GI law to transform indigenous heritage into protected and profitable market assets. The Bill also proposes establishing an Industrial Property Office to administer GI registration and includes provisions to prevent unfair competition and the deceptive use of geographical names.
But the government cannot afford to wait for enactment before beginning the preparatory work that will determine whether the new law has anything meaningful to protect. The most urgent task Nepal faces right now is not legislative. It is documentary. Before a single GI application can be filed, before a single product can be examined and registered, the evidence base must exist.
Geographic boundaries must be mapped. Traditional production methods must be recorded. Community histories of origin must be compiled. Product quality standards must be defined. This work must begin immediately, in parallel with the Bill's parliamentary passage, so that the moment the law creates a registration mechanism, Nepal's producers are ready to use it.
The government must launch a National Traditional Knowledge Documentation Initiative without delay, coordinated across the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, the Ministry of Industry Commerce and Supplies, the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, the Indigenous Nationalities Commission, and the National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities and Local Governments. This cannot be the work of one ministry acting alone. It requires field research, community consultation, geographic mapping, agricultural science, and legal analysis to work together systematically across all 59 indigenous nationalities and all ecological zones.
Non-governmental organisations and international NGOs working across Nepal's communities are essential partners in this effort and must be actively mobilised. They are already present in the villages where Dhaka is woven, in the tea gardens where Ilam farmers work, in the high-altitude communities where Yarsagumba is harvested, and in the community where Yomari is traditionally made.
Their field presence, community relationships, and research capacity can reach where government agencies cannot. WIPO’s traditional knowledge documentation guidelines provide a ready methodological framework that NGOs and research institutions can apply immediately. Local governments, empowered under Nepal’s federal structure, must also be formally directed and adequately resourced to participate.
What is needed now is the urgency to act, the coordination to document, and the institutional commitment to implement before the opportunity closes.
The question is not whether Nepal can protect Yomari. It never was. The question is whether Nepal will choose to protect it while there is still time.

title: Menschliche Originalität: Wie kreativ macht uns KI wirklich?
content:
Menschliche Originalität : Wie kreativ macht uns KI wirklich?
Künstliche Intelligenz hilft Menschen beim Schreiben von Büchern, Musik und Studien. Aber auch in überraschenden Bereichen hilft sie den Menschen über so manche Hemmschwelle hinweg.
Welchen Wert hat die Kunst? Interessanterweise war das für Ökonomen lange Zeit eher ein nebensächliches Thema. Dabei sind Künstler – mögen es Schriftsteller, Bildhauer oder auch Theaterleute sein – im besten Fall Menschen mit innovativen und originellen Ideen. Darin unterscheiden sie sich gar nicht so sehr von einer Berufsgruppe, die Ökonomen stets brennend interessiert hat: den Unternehmern.
Nun haben die Künstler durchaus auch selbst dazu beigetragen, dass sich die Wirtschaftswelt eher wenig mit ihnen beschäftigt hat. In einem lesenswerten Aufsatz zum Wesen der Kreativität hat der Forscher David Galenson vor einigen Jahren festgestellt, dass Künstler schon immer darum bemüht waren, sich abzugrenzen. Exemplarisch dafür steht ein berühmter Ausspruch Vincent van Goghs, der 1884 an einen befreundeten Maler schrieb: „Die Kunst ist – obwohl sie von menschlichen Händen erstellt wird – nie nur ein Resultat dieser Hände allein, sondern stammt von einer tieferen Quelle in unseren Seelen.“
Diese tiefere Quelle kann seinem Verständnis nach Gott sein, was die Kunst in den Augen vieler Künstler schon immer zu etwas Übernatürlichem, zutiefst Besonderem gemacht hat. Vielleicht erklärt gerade das den Schock, den die Erfindung des Sprachroboters ChatGPT bei vielen kreativen Menschen ausgelöst hat: Plötzlich kann jeder kreativ sein. Nötig ist dafür allein das Formulieren eines einfachen „Prompts“, wie die Anweisungen heißen, die die Nutzer der Künstlichen Intelligenz (KI) geben.
Das mag manch ein Künstler als Beleidigung empfinden. Für den Durchschnittsmenschen ist es aber erfreulich. Der Industrieländer-Club OECD wertet regelmäßig die Auswirkungen Künstlicher Intelligenz auf verschiedene Felder wie Produktivität, Innovation und Kreativität aus. Im Jahr 2025 hat die Organisation festgestellt, was man schon aus anderen Bereichen kennt: Die KI kann unerfahrene Schreiber besser machen. In einem Experiment zum Verfassen von Kurzgeschichten wirkten diese Geschichten auf die Leser neuartiger und origineller, wenn KI dabei zum Einsatz kam. Vergleicht man allerdings eine Vielzahl von Kurzgeschichten miteinander, die auf diese Weise entstanden sind, so zeigt sich: Mochte die einzelne Geschichte origineller wirken, so war die Bandbreite dieser Originalität dann doch begrenzt. Sprich: Die Muster ähnelten einander, was kein Wunder ist. Schließlich bedienten sich ja alle des gleichen Rohmaterials, der Daten von ChatGPT.
Nun macht die KI beständig Fortschritte, das Manko ist heutzutage also womöglich nicht mehr so groß. Ein Experiment mit 600 Teilnehmern zeigt aber, wo mögliche Schwachstellen liegen. Noch scheint es so zu sein, dass erfahrene Schreiber eher an Originalität einbüßen, wenn sie in ihren Texten zu Teilen auf Künstliche Intelligenz vertrauen. Die Untersuchung eines Forscherteams der Universität Exeter aus dem Jahr 2024, in KI-Zeiten also vor einer halben Ewigkeit, stellte fest: Wer bereits vor dem Schreiben des ersten Satzes auf KI setzte, begrenzte sich durch diese Vorauswahl in der Art und Weise, wie er den Text formulieren würde.
Plakativ lässt sich das anhand eines Beispiels zeigen, das der amerikanische Neurowissenschaftler Adam Green so formuliert: „Menschen können aufgrund ihrer persönlichen Erfahrungen ungewöhnliche Assoziationen haben. So kann es sein, dass jemand eine Wassermelone mit Fußball assoziiert. Solche Assoziationen können bei jedem Menschen unterschiedlich sein.“ Diese Unterschiedlichkeit könne KI nur schwer abbilden, was ihre kreativen Fähigkeiten begrenze. Greens ganz praktischer Tipp lautet darum: immer zunächst mit eigenen Ideen beginnen und erst dann die KI hinzuziehen.
Bevor es aber nun zu negativ wird, sei auf andere erstaunliche Fortschritte verwiesen, in denen die KI Menschen tatsächlich kreativer und produktiver macht: Der Ausstoß wissenschaftlicher Studien zählt dazu. Er ist deutlich gestiegen. Das ließe sich leicht als Zeichen des Verfalls wissenschaftlicher Arbeitsweisen interpretieren, in denen man der KI die Schreibarbeit überlässt und ihren Einsatz zu vertuschen sucht. Doch Forscher haben eine andere Erklärung: Tatsächlich konnten vor allem jene Akademiker die Zahl ihrer Schriften steigern, die keine englischen Muttersprachler sind. Da Englisch aber die weltweit wichtigste Wissenschaftssprache ist, verschafft der Einsatz kluger Übersetzungsprogramme dem Rest der Welt etwas mehr Chancengleichheit.
In den Vereinigten Staaten wiederum gibt es eine interessante Art der Selbstermächtigung, die ebenfalls aus dem Aufkommen der KI resultiert: Dort hat sich die Zahl der Menschen, die ohne Hilfe eines Rechtsanwalts eine Klage einreichen, seit 2022 in etwa verdoppelt. Die Vermutung ist: Die KI hat beim Verfassen der Klage geholfen. Über die Erfolgsaussichten sagt dies allerdings noch nichts aus.
Eines fällt übrigens in fast allen kreativen Bereichen auf – egal, ob es nun um Texte oder gar um KI-generierte Musik geht: So gerne die Menschen selbst KI einsetzen, so wenig mögen sie es, wenn ihnen Musik oder Texte präsentiert werden, die allein durch Künstliche Intelligenz entstanden sind. Menschliche Originalität, so könnte man daraus schließen, hat noch immer einen Wert.

title: A fuoco l’Oasi Lipu Soglitelle a Villa Literno
content:
L’Oasi Lipu, in Campania, è stata colpita da un incendio a pochi giorni dal riconoscimento europeo dell’area con l’istituzione della Zona di protezione speciale (Zps). Il Coordinatore delle Guardie Lipu Paolella: “è bruciato un miracolo”
L’Oasi Lipu Soglitelle, nel territorio di Villa Literno, in Campania, è stato colpito da un incendio. Secondo quanto riferito dalla Lipu, le fiamme avrebbero interessato soltanto la strada di accesso all’area protetta, provocando però gravi danni al ponte, che era stato recentemente riparato. L’episodio arriva a pochi giorni dal riconoscimento europeo dell’area con l’istituzione della Zps, Zona di protezione speciale, nell’ambito della rete Natura 2000 e delle direttive europee Uccelli e Habitat.
L’oasi rappresenta uno dei simboli della trasformazione di un territorio segnato in passato da criminalità e degrado. La zona, ricorda la Lipu, era stata utilizzata per lo scarico illegale di rifiuti e per attività di bracconaggio ai danni degli uccelli migratori. Attraverso l’operazione “Volo Libero”, condotta insieme ai carabinieri forestali, l’area è stata progressivamente sottratta a queste pratiche e trasformata in una riserva naturale e in uno spazio dedicato alla tutela ambientale, all’educazione e alla fruizione pubblica.
Maurizio Paolella, Coordinatore Guardie Lipu Caserta ha scritto un lungo posto sui social in cui ha commentato: “Non è bruciata una sterpaglia. È bruciato un miracolo. Un pezzo di terra martoriata dalla camorra, dai veleni, dagli sversamenti, che finalmente stava tornando a vivere. Che era diventata ZPS – Zona di Protezione Speciale. Che era diventata Casa per centinaia di uccelli, per la natura, per i nostri figli. E guarda caso brucia PROPRIO ORA. Proprio dopo che è stata istituita la ZPS. Proprio dopo che quell’area ha iniziato ad avere regole, tutele, occhi addosso. (…) anno bruciato canneti, nidi, vite. Hanno bruciato il lavoro di volontari che da anni, gratis, sotto il sole, cercavano di restituirci un pezzo di paradiso rubato”.

title: Opera over Peter van Pels in Osnabrück, meer dan vriendje van Anne Frank
content: Honderd jaar na zijn geboorte gaat in zijn geboortestad Osnabrück een opera in première over Peter van Pels, de onderduiker uit het Achterhuis. Het muziekstuk moet laten zien dat hij meer was dan alleen het eerste vriendje van Anne Frank. "De uitdaging was om hem zijn eigen stem te geven." "Peter van Pels is een beroemd figuur dankzij het dagboek, maar weinig mensen weten dat hij uit Osnabrück komt", zegt initiatiefnemer Ulrich Mokrüsch, artistiek directeur van het Theater Osnabrück, tegen Duitse media. "Zelfs in de stad zelf weten maar weinig mensen dat." Peter van Pels werd er in 1926 geboren, 80 kilometer van de grens met Nederland. Uit angst voor het opkomende nazisme verhuisde het Joodse gezin in 1937 naar Amsterdam, waar zijn vader Hermann voor Otto Frank ging werken. In 1942 doken ze samen met de Franks en tandarts Fritz Pfeffer onder in het Achterhuis aan de Prinsengracht. Einde in Mauthausen De opera gaat expres verder dan alleen het stuk dat door Anne Frank werd vastgelegd. Een fictief verhaal, omdat er nauwelijks details over zijn leven voor en na het Achterhuis bekend zijn. Zo bestaat er maar één foto uit zijn tijd in Amsterdam. "Het was belangrijk voor ons om een breder verhaal te vertellen dan alleen dat uit het dagboek. Dat is het cruciale verschil: het is het hele verhaal, van Osnabrück, via zijn onderduikadres in Amsterdam helemaal tot Auschwitz en Mauthausen, tot aan zijn dood." Peter van Pels overleed aan alle ontberingen die hij had meegemaakt op 10 mei 1945, vijf dagen na de bevrijding van het concentratiekamp. Zijn ouders waren al maanden eerder door de nazi's vermoord. Anne's vader Otto was de enige van de acht onderduikers die de oorlog overleefde. Opera is volgens Mokrüsch de ideale kunstvorm om dit tragische verhaal te vertellen. "De grootsheid en schoonheid van deze vertelvorm doen recht aan de omvang van het onderwerp", meent hij. "Het is niet een saaie geschiedenisles die je uit morele verplichting moet doorstaan omdat het zo belangrijk is. Het is ook gewoon een fijne avond theater." Hij heeft dan ook 2000 schoolkinderen uit de stad uitgenodigd om langs te komen, zodat ook zij bekend raken met het verhaal en de bredere context. "15-jarigen, net zoals hij was", zegt Mokrüsch, die hoopt dat ze zich herkennen in Peters zoektocht naar een eigen identiteit. "Dit was natuurlijk ook een normaal tienerleven", vult hij aan. "We willen de mensen van wie de levens verwoest werden laten zien als meer dan alleen slachtoffers." De bewoners van het Achterhuis waren volgens hem ook slechts "heel normale mensen in vreselijke tijden". "We hebben het voorrecht op te groeien in totaal andere tijden." Toch klinken de echo's van het verleden steeds luider door, nu in Duitsland de radicaal-rechtse AfD zo succesvol is. Mokrüsch noemt het fortuinlijk dat het stuk daarmee ook actueel is geworden. "We hadden niet kunnen bevroeden dat dit verhaal, over hoe om te gaan met de herinneringscultuur, steeds belangrijker zou worden." Geïnteresseerd in de Tweede Wereldoorlog? Abonneer je dan hier op onze nieuwsbrief.

title: Cómo conseguir el 33% de discapacidad de forma directa si ya tienes reconocida la dependencia
content:
Cómo conseguir el 33% de discapacidad de forma directa si ya tienes reconocida la dependencia
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
El nuevo marco normativo instaura una pasarela directa entre la Ley de Dependencia y el reconocimiento del grado de discapacidad
Durante años, una de las mayores distorsiones del sistema de protección social en España ha sido la existencia de la conocida como doble ventanilla. Este sistema hacía que familias y personas mayores que acababan de lograr el reconocimiento de la Ley de Dependencia se vieran obligadas a iniciar desde cero un segundo trámite de listas de espera para obtener el grado de discapacidad.
Sin embargo, gracias a la reforma aprobada por las Cortes y promovida desde el Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, se instaura la pasarela automática entre la Ley de Dependencia y el grado de discapacidad. De este modo, se eliminan duplicidades y se acortan los trámites administrativos necesarios para obtener la dependencia.
¿Cómo funciona la pasarela directa?
El principio de la norma se basa en un axioma de pura lógica: toda persona en situación de dependencia tiene, de facto, una discapacidad. A partir de la entrada en vigor del nuevo marco regulatorio, el reconocimiento de la dependencia da derecho automático a unos determinados porcentajes de discapacidad.
Con una dependencia de Grado I, la dependencia moderada, se alcanza de forma directa una discapacidad del 33%. En caso de tener un Grado II, o dependencia severa, se reconoce de manera automática un 65% de discapacidad. Si el usuario tiene reconocido un Grado III, o gran dependencia, el sistema le asignará un 65% de discapacidad sin necesidad de ningún trámite adicional.
No obstante, estos porcentajes no son definitivos. Si una persona con Grado I de dependencia considera que le corresponde un porcentaje de discapacidad superior al 33% -por ejemplo, un 45% o un 50%- tiene el derecho a acudir a la vía ordinaria del Centro Base para someterse a la valoración complementaria.
Ventajas de tener el 33% o el 65% de discapacidad
Esta equiparación directa ahorra hasta dos años de esperas y abre el acceso a un paquete integral de derechos fiscales y económicos. Para las personas un con grado de discapacidad a partir del 33%, esto supone el aumento del mínimo personal y familiar exento del IRPF, el acceso al IVA superreducido del 4% en la compra o adaptación de vehículos, bonificaciones en impuestos municipales y la reserva de plazas de empleo en convocatorias públicas.
Las ventajas a partir del 65% de discapacidad son aún mayores: mayor deducción en la declaración de la Renta; derecho a percibir una pensión no contributiva por invalidez; la exención total del impuesto de matriculación de vehículos y el derecho a múltiples bonificaciones autonómicas en transporte público y suministros.
¿Cómo solicitar la convalidación teniendo ya la dependencia?
Para quienes obtengan la resolución de dependencia tras la aprobación de la reforma, el volcado entre registros autonómicos será interno y automático. Para quien ya contaba con un grado de dependencia reconocido de forma previa, el procedimiento simplificado se tramita en tres pasos.
El primero es localizar la resolución oficial de dependencia expedida por la Consejería de Servicios Sociales de la comunidad autónoma. En dicho documento figura el grado de dependencia que le ha sido reconocido al usuario. Una vez en posesión de esta resolución, es necesario presentar la solicitud de homologación. Para ello, hay que acudir a la oficina de atención ciudadana, al Centro Base de Discapacidad o a la Sede Electrónica de la comunidad autónoma y rellenar el formulario titulado “Pasarela automática de reconocimiento de discapacidad por dependencia”. No requiere aportar informes médicos nuevos.
Por último, el organismo emitirá una solución administrativa de la discapacidad de forma directa y le enviará al usuario por correo postal la Tarjeta Acreditativa del Grado de Discapacidad para empezar a disfrutar de las ventajas fiscales.

title: Ethiopia’s Fields Are Becoming a Laboratory for Africa’s Next Agricultural Revolution
content:
Ethiopia’s Fields Are Becoming a Laboratory for Africa’s Next Agricultural Revolution
Addis Ababa, September 21, 2026 (FMC) — Some agricultural transformations are measured in harvests. Others are measured in the number of assumptions they force an entire sector to reconsider.
Across Ethiopia, an increasingly important experiment has been unfolding not inside a single research station or demonstration plot, but across millions of hectares: what happens when improved varieties, irrigation, mechanization, cluster farming, extension systems, climate information and new production practices are taken from the laboratory and pushed toward national scale?
The answer is beginning to reshape the country’s agricultural trajectory—and to attract attention well beyond its borders.
The transformation is particularly visible in wheat. Ethiopia’s rapid expansion of irrigated wheat production brought together several elements that are often treated separately in agricultural development: heat-tolerant varieties, irrigation, improved agronomic practices, organized production, research, extension and market linkages. By 2023, heat-tolerant irrigated wheat production had reached about one million hectares, with average productivity of around four tonnes per hectare, according to research documented through the FAO agricultural knowledge platform. The approach was identified as having potential relevance for wider African food-security efforts.
That is what makes the Ethiopian experience more consequential than a single crop story.
The country has increasingly been using agriculture as a field for systems integration—bringing technologies, institutions and production models together and testing what happens when they operate at scale.
Cluster farming is one such experiment. Rather than leaving millions of smallholders to confront modern agricultural markets and technologies individually, production is increasingly organized around coordinated areas and common production practices. Ethiopia says its cluster-farming system now involves about 9.5 million farmers cultivating 12.8 million hectares, with reported gains in productivity and farmer incomes.
Irrigation represents another major shift.
For generations, much of Ethiopian agriculture has been tied closely to the rhythm of seasonal rainfall. Expanding irrigation changes that equation by allowing farmers to manage water rather than simply wait for it. It can create additional production seasons, diversify crops and reduce exposure to erratic rainfall. The World Bank has identified irrigation as a central pathway for increasing agricultural productivity and strengthening food security in Ethiopia, including through multiple cropping seasons and greater production of diverse and drought-resistant crops.
The significance is not simply that more land is being irrigated.
It is that the production calendar itself can be redesigned.
The same logic extends to seeds. Improved varieties adapted to different agro-ecological conditions—including heat-tolerant wheat—are allowing production systems to move into environments once considered considerably more difficult. Research on Ethiopia’s irrigated wheat expansion has highlighted the role of improved varieties, cluster farming, research institutions, extension services and private-sector actors in bringing these technologies together at scale.
Mechanization adds another layer.
Agricultural modernization cannot be reduced to putting tractors into fields. It involves changing the economics and timing of land preparation, planting, harvesting, threshing, transport and post-harvest handling. Ethiopia’s agricultural development priorities explicitly include expanding mechanization alongside irrigation, horticulture, private-sector participation and institutional capacity.
And increasingly, the experiment is becoming digital.
Weather and climate information, for example, can become a production input in its own right. Research involving Ethiopian farming households found that access to weather and climate services was associated with productivity increases of 27 percent for maize and 17 percent for wheat, underscoring the potential value of information alongside physical inputs such as fertilizer and improved seed.
Taken together, these developments point toward a different understanding of agricultural innovation.
The important question is no longer only whether Ethiopia can produce a better seed, introduce a new machine, expand irrigation or teach a better farming technique. The larger question is whether these components can be assembled into a functioning production system and reproduced at national scale.
That is where Ethiopia’s agricultural experience becomes potentially continental in significance.
Africa does not lack agricultural potential. It has land, water, diverse agro-ecologies, a vast farming population and enormous domestic and regional markets. What has often been missing is the capacity to convert those assets consistently into productivity, reliable supply, commercial value and food-system resilience.
Ethiopia’s ongoing experiment is therefore less about discovering one magical agricultural solution than about testing how several solutions can work together.
Its emerging model is built around a simple but powerful proposition: productivity can be engineered.
Water can be managed. Production seasons can be extended. Varieties can be adapted. Farms can be organized. Information can reach farmers. Machinery can reduce bottlenecks. Research can feed directly into production. Markets can pull output through the value chain.
None of these changes eliminates the country’s agricultural challenges. Ethiopia still faces droughts, floods, pests, conflict-related disruptions, market constraints and serious food-security problems in vulnerable areas. FAO continues to report significant food-security pressures, particularly in pastoral regions affected by climatic and economic shocks.
But precisely because the challenges remain, the scale of the agricultural experiment matters.
Ethiopia is testing whether a predominantly smallholder agricultural economy can progressively move from vulnerability toward greater productivity, diversification and resilience without waiting for every constraint to disappear first.
That makes the Ethiopian countryside something more than the traditional backdrop to a national development story.
It is becoming a living testing ground for African agricultural transformation.
The most consequential harvest may therefore not be measured only in tonnes of wheat, maize, coffee or other crops. It may be measured in knowledge: which technologies work in which environments, which production systems can scale, which institutional arrangements improve farmer productivity, and which combinations can turn Africa’s enormous agricultural potential into dependable food and economic capacity.
If those lessons can travel—from Ethiopia’s irrigated lowlands to other African production zones, from research institutions to farmers, and from individual crops to entire food systems—the experiment taking place in Ethiopian fields could ultimately become part of something much larger.
Not simply an agricultural transformation in one country.
A laboratory for the continent.

title: California Tribes receive beach and ancestral village site back from transportation authority
content:
- The U.S. state of California has returned 55 hectares (136 acres) of Northern California coastline, including Blues Beach and the village site of K’etim, to three Coastal Yuki tribes.
- It is the first land Caltrans, the state transportation department, has ever returned to Indigenous ownership.
- Tribes first asked for the site in 2005, after learning looters were digging into archaeological sites and uncovering ancestral remains.
- The tribe hopes to use the land for education and gatherings, but the beach will remain open to the public.
On the Northern California coast, where the tall trees meet the sea, ancestors of the Coast Yuki people lie buried in an old village site above the bluffs in the U.S. state. Yet despite its cultural significance, the land has been owned by the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) until very recently.
A deed recorded July 6 transferred 55 hectares (136 acres) of that coastline to Kai Poma, a nonprofit founded by representatives of the Coyote Valley Band of Pomo Indians, the Round Valley Indian Tribes and the Sherwood Valley Band of Pomo Indians, the Ancestral Descendants of Coastal Yuki and Yuki.
It is the first time land held by Caltrans has been returned to Indigenous ownership, according to Kai Poma.
“We always felt this was ours,” Eddie Knight, chairman of Kai Poma and historic preservation officer for Coyote Valley Band of Pomo Indians, who is of Coastal Yuki descent, told Mongabay. “It may have been owned privately by somebody, but we still knew it was ours.”
The property sits just south of the small community of Westport, California, about 187 miles (300 kilometers) north of San Francisco. Visitors know the beach here as Blues Beach, but a major village site there is called K’etim by the Coast Yuki and Pomo lineages.
K’etim, according to the tribe’s traditional stories, is “where Seaweed Woman who lived at Mussel Rock met and fell in love with Coyote,” Kai Poma explained in a press release. This origin story “explains the creation of the coastline and its people. These teachings remain alive through the descendants who continue to revere, gather, camp, commune with, and steward their ancestral places.”
In 2005, word reached Knight and others that looters were digging at K’etim and uncovering human and archeological remains. “K’etim has endured substantial damage from off-road vehicle activity and widespread looting of archaeological sites,” Kai Poma stated.
In response, members of Sherwood Valley and Coyote Valley wrote to Caltrans that year asking for stewardship of the site and were granted a meeting. When the land was not handed over, Knight said, “we just kept on being persistent and said ‘give it to us.’”
It took many years of relentless efforts and a new law to make the transfer a reality. In 2021, Senator Mike McGuire wrote Senate Bill 231, specifically authorizing Caltrans to transfer Blues Beach “at no cost to a qualified nonprofit corporation.”
The three tribes formed the non-profit organization Kai Poma to receive the land.
The law requires Kai Poma to keep the land open to the public free of charge, bars commercial development, and returns the land to Caltrans if the nonprofit fails to maintain it or dissolves.
“This is beyond huge,” J. Carlos Rivera, tribal chairman of the Sherwood Valley Band of Pomo Indians, told the Los Angeles Times. “It’s enormous from our tribal perspective that we are basically obtaining the land that our people once lived on before colonization.”
The land is made up of about a half mile (800 meters) of beach, a terrace above the beach of roughly 40 hectares (100 acres), “which has our archaeological sites under it,” Knight said, as well as 16 hectares (40 acres) of old grazing land sloping from Highway 1 down to the ocean.
The sloping ground is the part Kai Poma can build on. Future management plans still need to be agreed upon by the three tribes, but Knight raised the possibility of building a traditional roundhouse, holding ceremonies and hosting an educational program.
The beach will remain open to the public. Cars have been prohibited from the beach by Caltrans but that rule was not strictly enforced. Kai Poma is still deciding how they will manage these issues.
“We want to protect the natural habitat,” Knight said. And to educate youth on “how to harvest our native foods, our sea foods, our seaweeds, our kelps and how to fish. Allowing our youth to get an idea of how they can use it in the future and use it now. It’s going to take a little time, but we do have a plan.”
The nonprofit has held a grant since 2023 for an archaeological survey to identify every site on the property, but could not begin the work, Knight said, until they had secured the deed. Now they plan to move forward and are planning a celebration and ceremony for all eight bands in Mendocino County.
This deed transfer is part of a larger Land Back movement: The push to return land to tribes, Traditional Owners and ancestral descendants of the land.
California has returned tens of thousands of acres to tribes in the past two years. The Yurok Tribe reclaimed more than 19,000 hectares (47,000 acres) along the lower Klamath River, the largest land return in state history. The Tule River Indian Tribe regained 6,890 hectares (17,030 acres) in Tulare County, and the Washoe Tribe of Nevada and California reacquired 4,158 hectares (10,274 acres) of former Sierra Nevada ranchland.
“136 acres of coastal lands have now been officially transferred into tribal stewardship, forever protecting one of the most spectacular stretches of the Mendocino Coast,” McGuire said in a statement. “This agreement, the first of its kind in California, gives the Sherwood Valley Band of Pomo Indians, Round Valley Indian Tribes and Coyote Valley Band of Pomo Indians the rightful opportunity to reclaim sacred lands and cultural traditions on this special piece of earth. And it’s about damn time.”

title: “Un kilómetro de humanidad”, la propuesta de un arquitecto mexicano presentada en El Salvador
content:
“Un kilómetro de humanidad”, la propuesta de un arquitecto mexicano presentada en El Salvador
El arquitecto mexicano Rafael Hernández Monroy presentó en el Foro Mundial de la Bicicleta una reflexión que busca cambiar la manera de entender la movilidad. Te contamos los detalles
Un kilómetro son 1,000 metros. La medida no cambia, pero recorrer esa distancia puede convertirse en una experiencia completamente diferente dependiendo de quién lo haga.
Esa premisa llevó al arquitecto mexicano Rafael Hernández Monroy a plantear una pregunta aparentemente sencilla, ¿cuánto mide un kilómetro de humanidad?
El profesional llevó trajo esa interrogante hasta El Salvador, donde participó en el Foro Mundial de la Bicicleta para compartir su experiencia en urbanismo y algunos de los proyectos desarrollados en México.
Su propuesta parte de colocar a las personas en el centro de la planificación de las ciudades. Un niño que camina hacia la escuela, un adulto mayor, una persona que utiliza silla de ruedas o alguien que se desplaza en bicicleta pueden recorrer el mismo kilómetro, pero las condiciones de la calle determinarán qué tan difícil, seguro o accesible resulta hacerlo.
Elementos tan cotidianos como disponer de un cruce seguro, encontrar árboles que proporcionen sombra, contar con un espacio para descansar o poder desplazarse sin temor terminan cambiando la experiencia.
“Siempre se ha enfocado el desarrollo en creer que entre más infraestructura construyamos, entre más le entreguemos nuestra ciudad al automóvil, es desarrollo”, explicó Hernández Monroy a elsalvador.com.
Para él, la prioridad debería ser distinta. “La ciudad debe ser para el peatón”, sostuvo.
Entre las soluciones que plantea están la construcción de aceras seguras, ciclovías y zonas peatonales, pero también un cambio en la forma en que ciudadanos y autoridades imaginan los espacios que ya existen.
De un camellón a un parque lineal
Durante su participación en el Foro Mundial de la Bicicleta, Hernández Monroy mostró ejemplos de los denominados “imaginarios urbanos” que ha desarrollado en Atlacomulco. La idea consiste en tomar fotografías de espacios reales y, mediante representaciones digitales, mostrar cómo podrían transformarse aplicando otras propuestas urbanísticas.
Uno de los ejemplos presentados corresponde a un camellón que actualmente divide una vialidad y que, bajo esa propuesta conceptual, podría convertirse en un parque lineal con áreas para caminar, utilizar la bicicleta y encontrarse con otras personas.
No se trata únicamente de mostrar una imagen atractiva, explicó, sino de provocar una conversación entre los habitantes sobre las posibilidades de transformar su entorno.
“Siempre nos conformamos con lo mismo de siempre, pero ya vimos que podemos tener una mejor ciudad”, comentó al explicar el propósito de estos ejercicios.
La experiencia que originó la pregunta
“Kilómetros de Humanidad”, sin embargo, no nació únicamente de su trabajo como arquitecto. La idea comenzó durante un viaje que Hernández Monroy realizaba por Centroamérica. Se encontraba en Costa Rica y pretendía llegar por tierra hasta Guatemala, pero al arribar a la frontera con Nicaragua descubrió que necesitaba una visa para ingresar.
Ante la imposibilidad de continuar inmediatamente, decidió caminar desde la frontera hacia el poblado costarricense de Los Chiles.
Durante el recorrido encontró un puesto de atención a refugiados de UNICEF, donde, según relató, le proporcionaron comida, agua, internet e incluso le ofrecieron hospedaje. Finalmente, él tuvo una alternativa, regresar a San José, comprar un boleto de avión y continuar su viaje.
Otras personas que encontró durante aquella experiencia no tenían esa posibilidad. Esa diferencia cambió la forma en que comenzó a pensar las distancias.
Mientras para él desplazarse era consecuencia de una decisión personal y disponía de recursos para modificar su ruta, para otras personas recorrer cientos o miles de kilómetros puede estar relacionado con situaciones como violencia, pobreza o desplazamiento. Fue entonces cuando la medida física dejó de ser suficiente.
¿Cuánta humanidad cabe en un kilómetro?
Con el tiempo, el propio arquitecto reformuló la pregunta que dio nombre a su proyecto. “La pregunta real creo que siempre estuvo mal hecha. No es cuánto mide un kilómetro de Humanidad, es cuánta humanidad se puede instaurar en un kilómetro”, afirmó.
Para Hernández Monroy, la respuesta puede encontrarse observando cómo se construye una calle y preguntándose quiénes realmente pueden utilizarla. Una acera demasiado estrecha, por ejemplo, puede representar un obstáculo para cualquier peatón y convertirse directamente en una barrera para alguien que utiliza silla de ruedas.
Lo mismo ocurre con los entornos escolares. El arquitecto plantea pensar en espacios suficientemente seguros para facilitar que los niños puedan desplazarse entre sus viviendas y centros educativos.
Durante su visita, Hernández Monroy también destacó la recuperación de espacios públicos que observó en San Salvador y consideró que la realización del Foro Mundial de la Bicicleta contribuye a colocar en la discusión regional formas de movilidad distintas al automóvil.
Al final, su propuesta plantea otra manera de evaluar el desarrollo urbano, no observar solamente cuánta infraestructura tiene una ciudad, sino preguntarse para quién fue construida. “Cuando hablamos de ciudadanos hablamos de todos”, resumió.

title: ONG alertan que miles de venezolanos se enfrentan a consecuencias a largo plazo tras los terremotos
content:
Las ONG del Comité de Emergencia Español han alertado de que, a medida que la respuesta a los terremotos que azotaron el centro y norte de Venezuela avanza hacia una fase de recuperación temprana, "miles de personas se enfrentan a las consecuencias a largo plazo del desastre, agravadas por las fuertes lluvias y el inicio del retorno a las aulas".
La organización se activó el pasado 25 de junio para responder a esta grave emergencia, con la participación de ocho ONG --Acción contra el Hambre, Aldeas Infantiles SOS, Educo, Entreculturas, Médicos del Mundo, Oxfam Intermón, Plan International y World Vision-- que "continúan trabajando de manera multisectorial en las regiones más afectadas, incluyendo el Distrito Capital, La Guaira, Miranda y Falcón, con planes de expansión hacia Carabobo y Aragua".
El Comité de Emergencia Español señaló que "la protección infantil, la continuidad educativa, la salud mental y la atención primaria de salud, vivienda, agua, saneamiento e higiene y asistencia alimentaria" constituyen "las prioridades absolutas en este momento" de la emergencia.
La organización destacó que el regreso a la actividad escolar ilustra la complejidad de la situación actual, ya que "la comunidad educativa requiere urgentemente de protocolos claros de actuación, rutas de evacuación y espacios preparados que eviten la toma de decisiones improvisadas ante posibles réplicas y que, al mismo tiempo, contengan las secuelas emocionales y el duelo de los estudiantes".
El Comité precisó que "para garantizar la dignidad, la autonomía y la capacidad de resiliencia de la población en situación de mayor vulnerabilidad, los esfuerzos de las 8 ONG internacionales especialistas en ayuda humanitaria" se articulan en torno a necesidades estructurales específicas de protección y acompañamiento psicosocial.
En materia de agua y saneamiento, la organización indicó que "tras haberse distribuido millones de litros de agua potable, las acciones se centran en el mantenimiento de infraestructuras esenciales en barrios y residencias de mayores, incluyendo la instalación de tanques, grifos y duchas inclusivas, así como el suministro de miles de kits de higiene familiar".
El Comité explicó que los programas educativos "permiten el reparto de kits de materiales, la reconstrucción de infraestructuras escolares dañadas y el diseño de modalidades híbridas o semipresenciales para facilitar el retorno seguro de más de 26.500 estudiantes, junto con la creación de espacios temporales de aprendizaje".
La organización señaló que en materia de asistencia sanitaria "se desarrollan jornadas móviles de atención médica y nutrición, soporte especializado para madres y bebés, y entrega de ayuda de primera necesidad, como alimentos y medicamentos", además de acompañamiento para restablecer medios de subsistencia.
La directora del Comité de Emergencia Español, Sara Barbeira, subrayó que "la reconstrucción trasciende a la entrega de ayuda material inmediata" y "exige un compromiso sostenido en el tiempo que dote a la ciudadanía y líderes comunitarios de las herramientas logísticas y emocionales necesarias para organizar la respuesta de sus propias comunidades".
Barbeira concluyó que "las necesidades sobre el terreno continúan en Venezuela" y ha apelado a mantener el apoyo, afirmando que "para que las familias en situación de mayor vulnerabilidad reconstruyan sus vidas y recuperen su independencia, el apoyo sostenido es indispensable".

title: Sacred springs of South Africa—pure waters or polluted? We found tiny bits of plastic in the samples we tested
content:
Across South Africa, natural springs are more than sources of freshwater. Some are places of healing, spiritual cleansing and rituals, where communities collect water and maintain longstanding cultural connections with the environment. For example, during cleansing rituals, people bathe in or collect spring water as a way of seeking spiritual renewal, healing and protection. These are known as sacred springs.
We are a team of environmental scientists and freshwater biologists interested in water quality, freshwater biodiversity and disturbances.
We set out to investigate an emerging form of pollution—microplastics—in nine sacred, unique and frequently visited freshwater springs in South Africa's Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal provinces.
We selected these springs because they are locally recognized as culturally and spiritually important, but before this study, scientists had not investigated whether they were polluted.
These sacred freshwater springs are quite remote and isolated. Still, our research found microplastics in all nine. We detected 184 particles in total, with concentrations ranging from 5 to 48 particles per liter.
There is no internationally agreed safe level of microplastics in freshwater or drinking water, so these concentrations cannot be described simply as "safe" or "unsafe." Results also vary because researchers use different methods to collect and test samples. A one-liter sample from these springs could therefore contain anywhere from just a handful to dozens of tiny plastic particles.
Although we cannot use this number alone to say whether the water is harmful to people, it shows that microplastic pollution is present and gives scientists a starting point for tracking whether the problem increases or decreases over time.
Our findings highlight that even sacred springs thought to be pristine contained microplastics. This could harm aquatic life, diminish the waters' spiritual value and expose people who drink, collect or bathe in them. This shows the urgent need for broader water-quality monitoring of sacred springs across South Africa.
How plastic particles polluted the heart of sacred water sources
We investigated the sulfur-rich springs at Isinuka, near Port St. Johns, Eastern Cape, and freshwater systems at sites in Mbizana, Eastern Cape, and Bongwana, KwaZulu-Natal, where naturally occurring carbon dioxide (CO₂) enters the water. In simple terms, CO₂ naturally escapes from underground through cracks and fractures in the rocks, mixing with groundwater before it reaches the surface.
The Bongwana springs lie along a major crack in Earth called the Bongwana Fault, which allows gas and groundwater from deep underground to rise to the surface. This makes the springs rare and scientifically important.
Sacred springs may seem protected because many are in rural or undeveloped areas. But they are still affected by what happens around them. Plastic waste left on land can break into tiny pieces and be washed into the water when it rains. Plastic fibers can also travel through the air and fall into springs. Bottles and packaging used near the water may add more pollution.
The highest concentration was recorded at Isinuka Spring (also known as Isinuka Healing Spa or the naturally pink spring). Almost 70% of the transparent particles were fibers or filaments, likely from clothing and other textiles.
Hundreds of people visit Isinuka on a typical weekend. People have traveled there for generations for spiritual and physical healing, cleansing practices, water collection, tourism and small-scale commercial activities, including selling the water and mud to those who visit.
We do not know whether these activities caused the pollution because we could not trace where each piece of microplastic came from. But the large number of visitors and the presence of microplastics show why we need to investigate how microplastics are getting into heavily used sacred waters.
The other springs we visited in Mbizana and around Bongwana were generally smaller and used mainly by local communities. People visit them to collect water, carry out traditional and cultural practices, and experience the unusual bubbling produced by naturally occurring carbon dioxide.
Compared with Isinuka, we observed relatively little visible plastic waste around these sites, although microplastics were still detected in the water.
What communities think about the health and pollution risks
At the springs, we spoke with local community members about their experiences, beliefs and practices associated with the water. We also asked for their views on health and plastic pollution.
At Isinuka, people were collecting water and mud to sell and using the area for spiritual and traditional practices.
One of the vendors who sells spring water and mud at the site told us:
"I have used Isinuka's pinkish water and mud for years and have never experienced any related health problems."
The presence of microplastics does not mean that using the water will necessarily cause illness. However, where people drink, collect or bathe in spring water, it is important to understand how much exposure may occur and whether there are any associated health risks.
For some community members, the value of the Isinuka springs extends far beyond the physical properties of the water. One person explained:
"People come here because they believe in the healing power of the water. This place is important to our community and our traditions."
Another community member emphasized the responsibility to protect the site:
"We need to look after the spring because it is something we have inherited from our ancestors and should leave for the next generation."
When we asked community members why there was so little plastic litter around the carbon dioxide springs in Mbizana, one community member explained that people are encouraged to keep the springs clean:
"Plastic pollution is not really a problem here because we are encouraged to clean the springs after using them and to avoid littering. We always clean up when we visit, although sometimes other community members and visitors still leave trash behind."
Another community member said, "When people come here, they should respect the spring and take their trash with them when they leave."
This shows that communities already play an important role in caring for these sites. They also highlighted an important point: A spring can look clean while still containing microplastics that cannot be seen with the naked eye.
What needs to happen next
Our findings provide baseline evidence that microplastic pollution has reached sacred freshwater systems. Our next step is to determine where the particles come from, how their presence changes between seasons and whether they accumulate in sediments or aquatic organisms.
Protecting these springs means keeping them physically clean while preserving their ecological condition and cultural integrity. Scientists and government authorities can monitor pollution and investigate its sources.
Communities should be partners, bringing local knowledge and long-term observations together with scientific evidence. Communities and visitors can also reduce single-use plastics, take waste home and join cleanups.
Scientific evidence and community stewardship are both needed to keep these waters healthy and culturally meaningful for future generations.
