title: Youth-Led Forest Restoration Movement Traces Back to a 9-Year-Old’s Question About Climate Change
content:
A boy who learned about Wangari Maathai’s tree-planting legacy at age nine sparked a youth-led forest restoration movement now training over 100,000 young Climate Justice Ambassadors across 76 countries.
Youth-led forest restoration at Plant-for-the-Planet began in 2007, when nine-year-old Felix Finkbeiner in Germany learned about Kenyan Nobel laureate Wangari Maathai’s campaign planting 30 million trees across Africa. Struck by her message that trees serve as powerful allies against global warming, Finkbeiner proposed that every country commit to planting one million trees. By age 13, he stood before the United Nations General Assembly, raising that ambition to one trillion trees worldwide.
Nearly two decades later, youth-led forest restoration has grown from one child’s conviction into a global movement operating academies across 76 countries. More than 104,800 children and youth have become Climate Justice Ambassadors, trained to understand the climate crisis and empowered to fight for their future through tree planting, public speaking, and community organizing. The organization has facilitated more than 36 million trees planted directly through its own restoration projects, while its platform has funded over 107 million trees through partner organizations worldwide.
The model driving youth-led forest restoration rests on a simple premise: young people affected most by climate change deserve genuine agency in addressing it, not token participation. At Plant-for-the-Planet Academies, Ambassadors learn climate science, then apply that knowledge locally, giving speeches, organizing tree-planting events, and mobilizing their communities. This youth leadership extends into formal governance through the Global Ambassadors Council, the organization’s official youth leadership body shaping strategic direction.
Restoration work spans three countries, each addressing distinct ecological challenges. In Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula, youth-led forest restoration protects and regrows Mayan rainforest, with more than 17.8 million trees planted, two reserves under active patrol, and work underway establishing a jaguar wildlife corridor connecting fragmented habitat. In Ghana, community-based restoration addresses degradation across the Savannah Ecological Zone, tackling climate vulnerability and poverty simultaneously through Plant-for-Ghana. In Spain, restoration projects are reviving lost forest landscapes around Granada, Doñana, Madrid, and Barcelona.
Beyond planting trees directly, youth-led forest restoration extends its impact through free technology supporting restoration organizations worldwide. Forest Cloud provides funding, management, and monitoring tools for restoration projects at no cost to nonprofits and communities, and has already enabled more than 100 million trees to be funded through the platform. FireAlert monitors 1.6 billion hectares for wildfire risk, allowing rapid response before fires spread. TreeMapper helps organizations track restoration progress with scientific rigor, while SeedManager, still in development, will support biodiverse ecosystem restoration specifically.
This technology-sharing approach reflects a deliberate strategic shift. Rather than measuring success purely by trees planted, satellite imagery and hectare-based tracking now anchor the organization’s accountability, providing longer-term verification of genuine forest recovery rather than short-term planting counts alone. Free restoration advice and published research further extend support to restoration organizations beyond Plant-for-the-Planet’s own direct projects.
Youth-led forest restoration also encompasses direct policy advocacy. The organization pushes for policies enabling forest conservation and climate justice, including transparency initiatives like TFFF Watch, which monitors accountability within international rainforest funding mechanisms, and Tracer, a tool supporting deforestation-free supply chains under European Union regulations.
National entities extend this youth-led forest restoration model across eight countries with independent operations. Ghana’s affiliate has empowered 2,400 Climate Justice Ambassadors while planting over 227,000 trees. Spain’s chapter, active since 2013, has trained over 5,100 Ambassadors through 151 academies while planting more than 501,000 trees. Since 2015, Czechia has mobilized youth and national celebrities alike, engaging over 1,000 Ambassadors. Each national entity adapts the core model, youth empowerment paired with forest restoration, to its own climate and community context.
Corporate partnerships increasingly fund this expansion. Companies can grow dedicated forest plots, support deforestation-free supply chains, and educate their workforce on climate action through structured partnership programs. Change Chocolate, a fair-trade product line, generates revenue that directly supports community forest protection in tropical regions vulnerable to deforestation pressure.
What distinguishes youth-led forest restoration from conventional reforestation charities is this persistent emphasis on intergenerational leadership. Ambassadors don’t simply volunteer for adult-designed programs; they shape strategy through elected councils, speak at international forums, and carry restoration knowledge into their own communities as they grow into adulthood. Finkbeiner himself, once a nine-year-old inspired by a Nobel laureate’s tree-planting campaign, now leads an organization where the next generation of nine-year-olds continues that same cycle of learning and action.
Nearly twenty years after one child’s question about climate change reached a global stage, youth-led forest restoration demonstrates that meaningful climate action doesn’t require waiting for adulthood or institutional permission. It requires forests, young people willing to fight for them, and the tools to turn that determination into hectares of restored, thriving ecosystems.

title: GREEN LUNG BOOST: Turning the corner — steady revival of Nelson Mandela Bay’s oldest park
content:
The oldest public park in the Bay has seen better days, garnering a reputation for harbouring vagrants and criminals seeking to prey on unsuspecting visitors.
Much of the park’s assets and infrastructure, such as a public pool and various sports facilities, have fallen into disrepair due to theft, vandalism and neglect, adding to the stigma surrounding the once-beautiful public space.
However, over the past three years, thanks to some much-needed attention from volunteers and local businesses in the community, alongside strategic partnerships between private entities and public directorates, St George’s Park has slowly started to turn the corner.
The municipality has spent a tidy sum on security upgrades around the park, while interest groups like the Friends of St George’s Park have launched initiatives to get more feet through the gates. Now the ruling government coalition’s biggest political rival, the DA, is drawing up plans to turn it into “Gqeberha’s Central Park”.
Whether it be nostalgia, a sense of community, or a need to provide the city with a safe public space, it seems St George’s Park has managed to transcend political divides, and everyone wants to see the park restored to its former glory.
“We appreciate any attention the park gets, but we want to move away from the polarising nature of politics and we certainly don’t want the park to become a political tool. The park is more important than that, and we want it to become a space where everyone can come together,” said André Theron of the Friends of St George’s Park.
R100m revamp pledge
This comes after Democratic Alliance mayoral candidate Retief Odendaal and several senior party members pledged R100-million towards revamping the park and its facilities, should the party win the upcoming local government elections. They conducted an oversight visit to St George’s Park last week.
While the group looked at several decaying facilities, and wanted to lay the blame at the feet of the city’s current leadership, a conversation with Odendaal afterwards specifically focused on bringing communities together.
“The park is situated in one of the most densely populated regions of Nelson Mandela Bay, and we have a diverse mix of scholars, students, professionals and families that live around it. Regardless of their political affiliations, these people need a safe space to go outside, go for a walk, to kick a ball.
Gqeberha’s Central Park?
“St George’s Park can be that. It has the potential to become for Gqeberha what Central Park is to New York,” said Odendaal.
The park was first opened in 1861. At the time it was surrounded by the manor homes of the city’s wealthiest and most influential families.
It is home to Pearson Conservatory, imported from the UK and erected in 1882, while St George’s Park, the oldest cricket grounds on South African soil, opened its pitch in 1889.
Over the years, and with the development of the Central neighbourhood as Gqeberha’s business hub, several apartment blocks were constructed and the area around the park became more densely populated.
Recreational facilities had to be developed along with the surrounding area, and over time the park became home to lawn bowls clubs, tennis clubs, the Mannville open air theatre, the Prince Alfred’s Guard Memorial, a borehole project to supplement the city’s water supply, as well as play parks and expansive public gardens.
State of decline
Sadly, as Central steadily declined, the park became unsafe and a hive of criminal activity, in turn leading to the deterioration of its many assets.
A prime example is the St George’s public swimming pool.
First opened in 1937, the 150-foot (45m) pool hosted many swimming galas while the main stands were packed with spectators. It was also a popular destination for bathers who preferred the pool to the beach during the summer season.
That is hard to believe when looking at the current state of the pool complex.
Deep trenches run along the sides of the pool where thieves dug up the piping, while the diving boards are inaccessible after the metal stairs were also stripped. In the ablution blocks and dressing rooms, basins and urinals have been destroyed, weeds grow out of toilet bowls and walls are scorched where vagrants lit fires.
According to the DA’s spokesperson for Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture in Nelson Mandela Bay, Sebezile Rafani, the city has budgeted a paltry R900,000 towards the pool. However, there is no clear indication what the funds are for, and the money has never been spent.
Municipal spokesperson Sithembiso Soyaya said the city acknowledges the state of the pool and that steps are being taken towards its restoration.
“The municipality is in the process of acquiring the services of a suitably qualified service provider to conduct a professional assessment of the work required, including the associated costs. There are also challenges relating to underground water, which have an impact on the repair or possible reconstruction of the pool itself.”
With regards to the broader park issues, Soyaya said improved security and access control was a major step towards the St George’s revival.
“The fencing around the park was redone, which improved access control and strengthened security within the facility. This was followed by the deployment of security officers to patrol the area.”
Soyaya said the Parks and Cemeteries sub-directorate also conducts monthly grass cutting and general maintenance operations throughout the park.
While he did not disclose the cost of the fencing upgrade, Theron said this was one of the initiatives the Friends of St George’s Park appreciated a lot as it came at a “hefty cost”.
“Security remains the biggest priority, and the new fence and gates is a major boon for the park.
“Our teams have partnered with a local homeless shelter MES, and are working closely with city officials. We conduct regular clean-ups of gardens and flower beds. Besides beautification, this also removes possible hiding spots for criminals and their loot, further improving security.”
He said the next step would hopefully include CCTV systems and additional lighting throughout the park.
Over the three years since the Friends of St George’s Park was established, Theron said their biggest goal was to get more people into the park, which in turn played a role in driving out vagrants and criminal elements.
The friends established a well-supported weekly Park Run, and hosted several Silent Book Club events, while an art exhibition in collaboration with painter Wessel Kotzee in December 2025 brought upwards of 1,500 people to the Pearson Conservatory.
“The Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality appreciates the efforts of the Friends of St George’s Park and their cooperative relationship with the Municipality’s Parks and Cemeteries sub-directorate in contributing to the upkeep of the park,” Soyaya said.
“Public participation and partnerships with community organisations remain important in complementing the municipality’s efforts to maintain public facilities and open spaces,” he added. DM

title: O que é saúde mental climática. E o que fazer para cuidar dela
content: <_cdata>Enchentes, queimadas e deslizamentos deixam marcas na população que sofre com eventos extremos. Efeitos vão de ansiedade a sintomas pós-traumáticos Equipe do ICMBio apoiando ações de resgate aos desaparecidos em Petrópolis, no Rio de Janeiro, em fevereiro de 2022 Equipe APA Petrópolis / NGI Teresópolis A água começa a cair e, para muitos, parece ser apenas mais um dia de chuva. Para Mariane Friedrich, porém, hoje o som da água tem outro significado. Desde as enchentes que atingiram o Rio Grande do Sul em 2024, uma mudança no tempo pode ser suficiente para trazer de volta memórias que pareciam ter ficado para trás. “Toda vez que chove fico em pânico”, comenta Mariane, de 36 anos, que no período das enchentes morava no bairro Sarandi, em Porto Alegre, um dos mais afetados da capital gaúcha. “Tive que ficar fora de casa por quase 60 dias e, depois, quando pude retornar, tivemos que limpar tudo. Ver as coisas que havíamos perdido foi muito triste e apavorante e, alguns meses depois, quando estávamos reconstruindo tudo, ficamos sabendo que teríamos que abandonar nossas casas.” A casa pode ter sido limpa, os móveis substituídos e a rotina reconstruída, mas retomar a vida depois de uma catástrofe não significa recuperar a sensação de segurança. “Antigamente o barulho da chuva era calmante, hoje em dia é terrível, traz lembranças ruins.”, conta. Mariane já realizava tratamento para ansiedade e depressão antes das enchentes e, com a chegada das águas, as crises se intensificaram. Durante o período das intensas chuvas, ela ficou sem acompanhamento psicológico e, junto do impacto emocional, perdeu seus pertences e a moradia, deixando de ter o espaço que antes era conforto e segurança. Hoje, relata que ainda convive com as marcas deixadas pela tragédia e enfrenta dificuldades para acessar o atendimento de que necessita. “Eu fazia tratamento no posto de saúde e, depois da enchente, ficou um pouco complicado, pois o posto também foi afetado. Agora faz um ano que me mudei e o posto perto do meu apartamento está sem médico, então sigo sem tratamento”. Mas o impacto, segundo ela, não ficou restrito à experiência individual. Os vizinhos também enfrentaram as consequências emocionais da tragédia. “Todos os meus vizinhos ficaram muito abalados. Muitos também já tinham ansiedade e depressão e disseram que piorou bastante. Com certeza nos unimos muito. Se não fosse essa união, acho que teria sido bem pior.”, diz Mariane. A vida antes e depois do evento O relato mostra que a enchente não terminou quando a água recuou e, para a psicóloga Sheila Cardoso, que acompanhou pessoas afetadas pelo desastre, abrigos coletivos e voluntários envolvidos na reconstrução, o sofrimento pode perdurar e se expressar no desgaste mental no longo prazo. “Essas sensações como medo de novas chuvas, dificuldade para dormir, ansiedade, sentimento de impotência, pânico e outros sentimentos se projetam como sintomas pós traumáticos e afetam todos os envolvidos”, explica a especialista. Segundo a psicóloga, a experiência das enchentes também aparece nos relatos como um divisor na trajetória de quem passou pelo desastre. “Existe uma vida antes e uma vida depois”, observa. A frase aparece de diferentes formas nos relatos de pessoas que acompanhou. A enchente passa a ser uma referência temporal coletiva para reorganizar memórias, perdas e mudanças. Os números também ajudam a dimensionar aquilo que nem sempre aparece nas imagens de ruas alagadas e casas destruídas. Uma pesquisa do IBGE sobre as enchentes de 2024 mostrou que 67,5% dos moradores das áreas pesquisadas disseram ter tido a saúde mental abalada. Entre os domicílios atingidos, esse foi o impacto pessoal mais citado pelas famílias. Além dos sintomas traumáticos frequentemente observados em pessoas que tiveram suas casas e meios de vida afetados, eventos climáticos extremos podem produzir consequências que ultrapassam a experiência individual e atingem comunidades inteiras. O chamado Trauma Coletivo Climático é uma expressão utilizada para abordar os efeitos emocionais, psicológicos, sociais e comunitários produzidos quando uma população vivencia conjuntamente uma situação de desastre ou ameaça climática, para ampliar o olhar para além do sofrimento individual. Uma enchente, por exemplo, pode interromper relações de vizinhança, desestruturar atividades econômicas, deslocar famílias, interromper a rotina escolar de crianças e adolescentes e alterar a relação das pessoas com o próprio território. O mesmo pode acontecer em diferentes tipos de eventos extremos. Secas prolongadas podem comprometer o trabalho e a renda dos agricultores. Queimadas podem provocar perdas materiais, deslocamentos e medo recorrente. Deslizamentos podem retirar famílias de seus territórios. Ondas de calor também podem afetar de maneira desigual pessoas já expostas a condições de vulnerabilidade. O Ministério da Saúde já reconhece que eventos climáticos extremos podem causar sofrimento psicológico e impactos psicossociais que permanecem depois da ocorrência do desastre. Do trauma à política pública Esta realidade menos visível dos desastres climáticos é o que uma campanha chamada Saúde Mental Climática quer trazer para o debate público: o sofrimento emocional, psicossocial e comunitário provocado por eventos extremos. Para Luciana Brafman, fundadora da Time To Act e articuladora da campanha, a resposta aos desastres ainda deixa uma lacuna quando o assunto é o cuidado com a saúde mental. Luciana é advogada, produtora, diretora e ativista climática, e hoje atua como consultora da ONU para políticas públicas sobre clima, sustentabilidade e bem-estar das comunidades. Para ela, a reconstrução costuma se concentrar na recuperação de casas, estradas e equipamentos públicos, que ela afirma ser uma parte importante, mas o sofrimento emocional das pessoas e das comunidades às vezes é deixado de lado. “A Time to Act começou deste incômodo, de olhar para a crise climática por um lado humanitário. Eu observei um terremoto que ocorreu nas Filipinas em 2019 e mais de um ano e meio depois ainda havia muitas pessoas morando nas ruas em barracas. Isso desestrutura uma família inteira e tem impactos enormes no longo prazo, levou até ao agravamento da crise de opióides, isso mexeu muito comigo”, confessa Luciana. Ela conta que acompanhou as sucessivas chuvas que atingiram o Sul do país: “pensei, como um ser humano consegue passar por tudo isso, vizinhanças inteiras destruídas e depois sendo atingidas novamente em tão pouco tempo. Me vi naquelas pessoas e neste momento percebi a importância de um apoio psicossocial.” Assim, a mobilização passou a defender uma mudança na forma como o país responde aos eventos extremos. A proposta é incorporar a saúde mental ao planejamento das emergências climáticas, e não tratá-la apenas como uma resposta pontual depois que o desastre acontece. “Claro que o apoio inicial com alimentação e abrigo é fundamental, mas o lado psicológico também é importante. Fomos ao Rio Grande do Sul e fizemos entrevistas e as pessoas seguiam traumatizadas, muitas vezes sem nem perceber isso.” Ela comenta que para além de ver a situação como uma questão de saúde mental climática, é preciso observar o Trauma Coletivo Climático. “O SUS possui diretrizes para situações semelhantes, mas na minha visão era preciso uma prática coletiva. A ideia é trabalhar em conjunto com políticas públicas já existentes no Brasil e ampliar, fazer com que elas se encaixem nessas novas necessidades que vieram com as crises climáticas.” A discussão acabou por gerar o Projeto de Lei 6151/2025, de autoria dos deputados Pompeo de Mattos (PDT) e Fernanda Melchionna (PSOL), que segue em tramitação na Câmara dos Deputados e aguarda análise da Comissão de Integração Nacional e Desenvolvimento Regional. O PL propõe uma Política Nacional de Saúde Mental Climática e prevê ações de atenção psicossocial antes, durante e depois de eventos climáticos extremos. O que se busca é organizar uma resposta que acompanhe todo o ciclo do desastre, desde a preparação das equipes e das comunidades, passando pelo atendimento durante a emergência e pela continuidade do cuidado na fase de reconstrução. A proposta busca articular diferentes áreas do poder público, como saúde, assistência social, educação e defesa civil. Entre as diretrizes previstas estão a oferta de atendimento multiprofissional e de medidas de apoio que levem em conta as necessidades individuais e comunitárias, além da reconstrução de vínculos e do fortalecimento da vida comunitária. O público atendido não se restringiria às pessoas que apresentam sintomas após um desastre. O projeto prevê atenção a familiares, crianças, adolescentes, idosos, pessoas com deficiência, profissionais que atuam na linha de frente das emergências e comunidades expostas a riscos climáticos. A preparação de equipes, a identificação de populações vulneráveis, a criação de protocolos, o atendimento durante a emergência e o acompanhamento no período de reconstrução fariam parte de uma mesma política. A proposta também considera as diferentes condições de vulnerabilidade socioambiental dos territórios. Além disso, é apontada a criação de um Sistema Nacional de Saúde Mental Climática, para integrar serviços, produzir dados e articular ações entre saúde, assistência social, educação e outras áreas, e de Centros de Resiliência, Cura e Reconstrução de Comunidades, voltados ao atendimento especializado e à reconstrução emocional e comunitária após desastres.

title: Sign language access key to protect children with disability: Minister
content:
"Sign language enables individuals to build relationships, access information, learn, express themselves, voice opinions, make decisions on their own lives, and participate in social life. For deaf children, access to communication is not merely a technical issue but a fundamental part of fulfilling children's rights," she said in a statement on Thursday.
The minister made the statement during the 2026 International Day of Sign Languages Campaign.
Arifah noted that limited communication access can affect many areas of children's lives, from education and access to information to social interaction and self-expression.
Adequate communication access enables children to communicate when they feel scared, uncomfortable, or sick, and to speak up about bullying or violence, she added.
To this end, the ministry continues to advocate for equal access to women and child protection services, including through the SAPA 129 hotline for women and children with disabilities.
"We must ensure that every victim who wants to speak out has the means to report their experience. We must prevent children who experience violence from being unable to explain what happened simply because those around them cannot communicate with them," Arifah stated.
Therefore, disability-friendly services should not be viewed as mere add-ons. Instead, inclusivity must be an integral part of the service quality itself, she continued.
Meanwhile, Iwan Satriyawan Setyohadi, an Indonesian Sign Language instructor from the Indonesian Sign Language Center in Jakarta, explained that Indonesian Sign Language (Bisindo) is the natural language of the deaf community. It possesses distinct linguistic characteristics and is not universal.
Understanding deaf language and culture is crucial to establishing inclusive communication, he noted.
"By learning sign language, we not only gain the ability to communicate with deaf individuals but also learn to understand the culture and create a more inclusive environment. Sign language can serve as a bridge, enabling better communication between deaf individuals and the wider community," Iwan remarked.

title: Medellin Native David Velez to Invest US$1.58B in Colombia, Calls for End to Usury Cap
content:
David Velez, the Medellin-born founder and CEO of Nubank, plans to invest approximately US$1.58 billion in Colombia between 2026 and 2030 as the digital bank expands its presence in the country.
Velez announced the investment alongside Nu Colombia General Manager Marcela Torres and Colombia Fintech President Gabriel Santos, saying the company intends to remain in Colombia for the long term.
Nu entered Colombia in 2021 with a credit card and has since expanded its financial products. The company now holds more than US$3.49 billion in deposits across savings accounts and CDTs, or fixed-term deposit certificates.
Velez said Nu grew from zero to five million customers within five years, including customers who previously lacked access to credit, and that the company’s next goal is to become one of Colombia’s leading financial institutions.
The planned US$1.58 billion investment will focus on four areas: advanced data and artificial intelligence platforms, new financial services, expansion of strategic teams, and capital to support what Velez described as “responsible, scaled growth.”
How David Velez plans to expand Nubank in Colombia
Torres also presented figures on Nu’s position in Colombia’s banking sector, saying the company now has the fourth-largest base of individual deposits nationwide.
Nu currently holds roughly 10% of Colombia’s credit card market and about 7% of individual deposits, according to figures presented by the company. It has reached 6 million customers, equivalent to approximately 14% to 15% of Colombia’s adult population.
Torres said Nu’s credit card business is growing 60% year over year. She also argued that without the company’s growth, Colombia’s overall credit card market would have contracted.
According to Nu, nearly 40% of customers who joined the company over the past year had no previous relationship with Colombia’s financial sector.
The company also said it accounted for 25% of people who gained access to credit nationwide during the same period, despite holding about 10% of the credit card market.
Women represented 59% of those newly included customers, compared with what Nu described as a sector average of 41%.
Torres acknowledged that credit risk could increase as the company expands lending to populations that have historically had less access to the formal financial system.
Why David Velez wants to end Colombia’s usury cap
Velez also called for changes to Colombia’s usury rate, the maximum interest rate lenders are legally permitted to charge.
He described the cap as “the biggest obstacle to financial inclusion in Colombia,” arguing that it limits regulated financial institutions’ ability to lend to higher-risk customers.
According to Velez, only 20% of Colombia’s population has access to credit, leaving many others dependent on informal lenders, including those known as “gota a gota,” or daily-payment lenders.
He said interest rates charged by such lenders can range from 500% to 2,000%, while borrowers do not receive the consumer protections available through regulated financial institutions.
Velez argued that because regulated banks cannot price loans according to the risk associated with individual borrowers beyond the legal ceiling, lenders may reject higher-risk applicants rather than extend credit.
He proposed two possible changes. The first would end the practice of combining different credit products when calculating a single usury ceiling and instead establish separate limits for different types of credit.
The second would eliminate the interest rate cap altogether, a measure Velez argues would increase credit availability for consumers and small businesses.
Velez said he hopes Colombia’s next administration will address the issue, arguing that changes involving interest rates, reduced dependence on cash and faster implementation of open finance regulations could significantly accelerate financial inclusion.

title: Sustainability, Vol. 18, Pages 9749: Introducing Earthquake Preparedness from Early Childhood: The “Earthy and Quaky” Education Program as an Interdisciplinary and Learning Pathway Toward a Culture of Safety
content: Destructive earthquakes are natural hazards highlighting the importance of introducing disaster preparedness from early childhood. Preschool children require developmentally appropriate educational approaches that connect scientific understanding with experiential, play-based, and participatory learning. This study presents the design and implementation of the “Earthy and Quaky” (EQ) earthquake education program, developed for children aged 3–6 years and implemented in two preschool educational settings in Zografou City (Attica, Greece). The program was structured as an interdisciplinary and progressive learning pathway comprising eight thematic units integrating natural and social sciences, language, mathematics, music and movement, visual arts, puppet theater, simulation, and earthquake drills. Follow-up activities and family involvement extended learning beyond the classroom. The implementation involved 28 children, whose participation, verbal responses, interactions, behavioral responses, and drawings were qualitatively observed. The observations indicated active engagement with concepts, including the Earth’s structure, earthquake occurrence and impact, and self-protection practices. Within the context of this small-scale implementation, the observations indicate that an interdisciplinary, experiential, and activity-based framework can provide a supportive learning context for earthquake preparedness during preschool years. The adaptable structure, low-cost materials, repeated reinforcement, and school–family connection may offer potential for adaptation to other preschool contexts after studying applicability and effectiveness with larger and more diverse samples.

title: King Jaja’s challenge to Nigeria: Power, defiance and economic self-determination, by Dakuku Peterside
content:
If King Jaja of Opobo were alive today, where would he stand amid Nigeria’s diplomatic pressure, economic uncertainty and deepening social tension—and what would he do? Would he negotiate, confront, build, or turn adversity into leverage? History is most useful when it refuses to remain in the past. More than a century after Jaja’s rise, his story speaks urgently to Nigeria’s struggles over resources, independence and institution-building. What might Nigeria become if its leaders pursued economic agency with his strategic audacity?
The question gains resonance as Opobo Kingdom prepares for the coronation of His Majesty, King Charles Douglas MacPepple Jaja, Jeki VI, as Amanyanabo and Treaty King on September 26, 2026. Yet the finest tribute to Opobo’s legacy is to ask what Jaja’s example demands of a nation struggling to convert abundance into prosperity.
Jaja’s achievement was extraordinary not simply because he rose from adversity to become a powerful king and merchant, but because he understood the architecture of power. Palm oil was more than a commodity; it underwrote a political economy. Whoever controlled access to the hinterland, trading channels and terms of exchange possessed not only wealth, but leverage. From Opobo, Jaja organised people, secured routes, cultivated alliances and resisted European attempts to bypass African middlemen and dictate commercial terms. His struggle was not against international trade. It insisted that engagement must not become surrender and that partnership must not deprive a people of the right to defend their interests.
Here Jaja becomes a mirror for modern Nigeria. The commodities have changed; the questions have not. Who sets the terms on which Nigerian resources enter the world economy? Who owns the technology, finances production, processes raw materials and controls distribution? Who captures the value, and how much remains in Nigerian hands? Nigeria has too often mistaken possession for power. Producing crude oil is not controlling the petroleum value chain. Growing cocoa, sesame or cashew is not the same as processing, branding and distributing them. Mineral deposits do not guarantee prosperity. Resources become power only when knowledge, capital, infrastructure and institutions are organised around them.
Jaja understood that distinction in the nineteenth century; Nigeria still wrestles with it in the twenty-first. We export raw materials and talented people, then import finished goods, technology and expertise at a premium. A large market that mainly consumes what others produce is not yet an economic power; it is an opportunity captured by others.
Economic self-determination does not mean isolation or hostility to investment. Jaja traded internationally. The lesson is to engage with clarity and strength. Foreign capital should enlarge domestic capability, not replace it. Partnerships should leave skills, technology, supply chains and competitive Nigerian enterprises behind. Trade should bridge commerce and production. This requires more than patriotic rhetoric: it requires organisation. Jaja’s power rested on commercial networks, political relationships, rules and coordinated action. His story exposes Nigeria’s deeper contradiction. The country does not lack exceptional individuals; it lacks enough durable institutions to convert individual brilliance into collective progress.
Nigeria must convert population into human capital through education, health and technical competence. Transport and digital systems must connect producers to markets. Reliable energy must underpin the economy, not burden households and enterprises. Law must protect contracts and property. Policy must reward those who produce, innovate and employ. The lesson is especially urgent in the Niger Delta. The region that powered Nigeria’s palm-oil and petroleum economies remains scarred by pollution, poverty, unemployment and inadequate infrastructure. This is not merely a development failure; it is a moral contradiction. No region should indefinitely bear the costs of national wealth while receiving fragments of its productive promise.
Jaja’s arrest and exile in 1887 also warn that economic power is never uncontested. Nations with strategic territory, critical resources or large markets should expect pressure. The answer is neither theatrical defiance nor timid compliance, but intelligent statecraft: knowing what to defend, negotiate and build so engagement does not begin from weakness. Jaja should not be romanticised. No nineteenth-century order can simply be transplanted into a modern federation. History invites illumination, not imitation. Jaja shows that resilience means converting adversity into organised capacity. Leadership means using authority to expand a people’s agency.
The coronation of King Charles Douglas MacPepple Jaja, Jeki VI, invites national reflection. Jaja might recognise a gifted people operating below their collective power, a resource-rich nation capturing too little value and a sovereign state negotiating too often from dependence. He would understand that outrage without organisation changes little.
His challenge to this generation would not be to recreate his world, but to recover his imagination: to build institutions that outlive their founders, enterprises that compete globally and an economy that gives citizens a stake in prosperity. Jaja’s legacy remains unfinished because Nigeria must turn potential into power, resources into shared value and political independence into economic self-determination.
•Dr Peterside, Leadership Architect and Management Turnaround Expert, is the author of the book Leading in a Storm.

title: Μ. Χρυσοχοΐδης: Δημιουργείται Εθνικό Κέντρο Αντιμετώπισης της Απάτης
content:
13:30 22/09
Νέα πυρηνική συνεργασία ΗΠΑ-Τουρκίας για μικρούς αρθρωτούς αντιδραστήρες και αντιδραστήρες 4ης γενιάς
Μπαϊρακτάρ: "Θα διαφοροποιήσουμε το ενεργειακό μας μείγμα".
Τη δημιουργία Εθνικού Κέντρου Αντιμετώπισης της Απάτης, το οποίο θα ενταχθεί στην Υποδιεύθυνση Οικονομικής Αστυνομίας της Διεύθυνσης Αντιμετώπισης Οργανωμένου Εγκλήματος, ανακοίνωσε ο υπουργός Προστασίας του Πολίτη Μιχάλης Χρυσοχοΐδης, μιλώντας σήμερα το πρωί στον τηλεοπτικό σταθμό "ΣΚΑΪ".
Ο κ. Χρυσοχοΐδης αναφέρθηκε στην αντιμετώπιση των τηλεφωνικών και ηλεκτρονικών απατών, σημειώνοντας ότι οι αρμόδιοι αξιωματικοί του νέου κέντρου θα ασχολούνται συστηματικά με 13 δράσεις στις οποίες, όπως είπε, επικεντρώνονται οι κακοποιοί. Όπως σημείωσε, το ζήτημα των ηλεκτρονικών απατών βρίσκεται πλέον στο επίκεντρο, καθώς μέσω ηλεκτρονικών υπολογιστών παραβιάζονται λογαριασμοί και πιστωτικές κάρτες και αποσπώνται μεγάλα χρηματικά ποσά.
Ο υπουργός αναφέρθηκε επίσης στην υπόθεση του Αλκέτ Ριζάι και τη χορήγηση άδειας, στην ενδοοικογενειακή βία και την ανήλικη παραβατικότητα, καθώς και στην υπόθεση του θανάτου του Γιώργου Μαζωνάκη.
Αναλυτικά, ο κ. Χρυσοχοΐδης ανέφερε:
Για τις τηλεφωνικές και ηλεκτρονικές απάτες
"Αυτή τη στιγμή κυριαρχούν οι τηλεφωνικές απάτες, αλλά, πολύ σύντομα, η Αστυνομία θα τελειώσει με αυτό το φαινόμενο. Ωστόσο, έρχεται το άλλο το φαινόμενο, αυτό της ηλεκτρονικής απάτης, όπου εκεί παίζονται μεγαλύτερα ποσά, διακυβεύονται περιουσίες και αυτοί, οι οποίοι δραστηριοποιούνται σε αυτό αποκομίζουν πάρα πολλά χρήματα… Είναι άλλου είδους κακοποιοί πιο μορφωμένοι, πιο intellectual".
"Οι δράστες χακάρουν μέσω ηλεκτρονικών υπολογιστών τους λογαριασμούς των θυμάτων ή τις πιστωτικές τους κάρτες και αποσπούν χρήματα".
"Ήδη συλλαμβάνονται μαζικά συμμορίες που επιδίδονται σε τηλεφωνικές απάτες", ενώ, όπως σημείωσε, "το ζήτημα της ηλεκτρονικής απάτης τώρα αρχίζει να παίρνει διαστάσεις".
Για τη δημιουργία του νέου κέντρου
"Πριν από περίπου 15 μέρες, πραγματοποιήθηκε σύσκεψη, στο υπουργείο Προστασίας του Πολίτη, στην οποία συμμετείχαν αρμόδιοι από οργανισμούς, φορείς, τράπεζες και εταιρείες".
"Το Εθνικό Κέντρο Αντιμετώπισης της Απάτης, θα εντάσσεται στη Υποδιεύθυνση Οικονομικής Αστυνομίας της Διεύθυνσης Αντιμετώπισης Οργανωμένου Εγκλήματος και οι αρμόδιοι αξιωματικοί θα ασχολούνται συστηματικά με 13 δράσεις, στις οποίες φαίνεται ότι επικεντρώνονται οι κακοποιοί, ώστε να τις αντιμετωπίσουμε όλες".
Για την υπόθεση του Αλκέτ Ριζάι και την κριτική που έχει ασκηθεί για τη χορήγηση άδειας στον βαρυποινίτη
"Δεκαέξι άδειες είχε πάρει ο Ριζάι. Αν θέλετε προσωπικά, θα διαφωνούσα να πάρει άδεια ο συγκεκριμένος, αλλά αυτό δεν είναι δικό μου θέμα. Είναι θέμα του νόμου".
"(Ο Ριζάι) Θα συλληφθεί, όπως συλλαμβάνονται όλοι. Όπως βλέπετε δεν υπάρχει τίποτα ανεξιχνίαστο. Καμιά δολοφονία χωρίς σύλληψη και προσαγωγή στον εισαγγελέα. Κανένα αδίκημα, το οποίο δεν εξιχνιάζεται. Συνεπώς, θα δείτε και στη συνέχεια πόσο αυτή η κεκτημένη ταχύτητα που έχει αποκτήσει η ελληνική αστυνομία με τις μεγάλες της υπηρεσίες, όπως είναι το λεγόμενο ελληνικό FBI, πόσες ακόμη επιτυχίες θα έχει, γιατί ακριβώς οι άνθρωποι εργάζονται καθημερινά αφοσιωμένα".
Για την ενδοοικογενειακή βία και την ανήλικη παραβατικότητα
"Αυτό που εμένα προσωπικά με απασχολεί ως πολιτικό προϊστάμενο της Αστυνομίας, με βάση αυτά που βλέπω, είναι το θέμα της βίας. Η βία έχει αυξηθεί πάρα πολύ".
"Κάθε βράδυ γίνονται 100 συλλήψεις (κακοποιητών) μέσα από 100 καταγγελίες. Οι συλλήψεις πέρυσι ήταν περίπου 35.000, εκ των οποίων οι μισές καταλήγουν στα δικαστήρια. Δηλαδή γύρω στις 14.000-15.000. Από αυτούς κάποιοι είναι έξω με περιοριστικούς όρους, κάποιοι είναι προφυλακισμένοι και κάποιοι είναι κατάδικοι. Αυτό οφείλεται στη δουλειά της αστυνομίας. Ένα μέρος από αυτούς είναι υπότροποι".
"Η βία στους ανήλικους υπήρχε πάντα. Αλλά όχι αυτού του επιπέδου και όχι αυτή η αγριότητα. Αυτά όμως δεν είναι αστυνομικά θέματα, αλλά έχουν να κάνουν με την οικογένεια, με την εκπαίδευση και καλούμαστε όλοι να τα διαχειριστούμε. Η αστυνομία έρχεται τελευταία για να προστατεύσει τη ζωή ενός παιδιού που ενδεχομένως υφίσταται μια επίθεση".
"Τι θα το κάνουμε ένα παιδί 13 χρόνων, που είναι εθισμένο στη βία, στην παραβατικότητα, θα το κλείσουμε στη φυλακή; Πώς αντιλαμβανόμαστε τη διαχείρισή του;".
"Η αστυνομία δεν διαπαιδαγωγεί. Παρ' όλα αυτά, πολλές φορές, πολλά παιδιά, μέσα από τις υπηρεσίες των ψυχολόγων της υπηρεσίας, βοηθούμε και τέτοια. Αλλά νομίζω ότι, βασικός παράγοντας είναι η οικογένεια γι' αυτό και έχει αυξηθεί πάρα πολύ η ποινή για όσους ασκούν επιμέλεια ανηλίκων".
Για την υπόθεση του θανάτου του Γιώργου Μαζωνάκη:
"Κάθε πτυχή αυτής της υπόθεσης ερευνάται και στο πεδίο του συγκεκριμένου γεγονότος, όπως και στο πεδίο της ευρύτερης δραστηριότητας γύρω από αυτά τα θέματα".
"(Στην αστυνομία πλέον) γίνονται πολύ καλύτερα τα πράγματα διότι προάγονται και επιλέγονται ικανοί άνθρωποι, υπάρχει αφοσίωση, στοχοπροσήλωση, όλες οι υπηρεσίες έχουν το αναγκαίο και κατάλληλο προσωπικό σε αριθμό, αλλά και σε ποιότητα, προκειμένου να διερευνούν υποθέσεις και να απαντούν στα όποια μεγάλα εγκλήματα εμφανίζονται καθημερινά".
"(Διαθέτουν) σημαντικά τεχνολογικά μέσα. Δείτε για παράδειγμα τη Διεύθυνση Εγκληματολογικών Ερευνών, ας πούμε το ελληνικό CSI, υπάρχουν οι αστυνομικοί που αναλύουν τα ψηφιακά ίχνη, οι οποίοι είναι εκπληκτικοί, πολύ υψηλού επίπεδου επιστήμονες, οι οποίοι είδατε σε πόσες λίγες ώρες έκαναν ανάκτηση δεδομένων…".

title: Cães-selvagens vivem 'odisseia' percorrem 4 mil km e quebram recorde entre mamíferos africanos
content:
Cães-selvagens-africanos: espécie ameaçada é conhecida pela resistência e capacidade de percorrer grandes distâncias (Pexels)
Redatora
Publicado em 19 de setembro de 2026 às 06h35.
Três cães-selvagens-africanos percorreram 4.126 quilômetros pela Zâmbia, estabelecendo a maior rota de dispersão já registrada para um mamífero da África. A "odisseia", acompanhada por pesquisadores durante meses, revelou a capacidade desses animais de atravessar grandes áreas em busca de novos territórios e oportunidades de reprodução.
O deslocamento foi descrito em um estudo publicado na última quarta-feira, 9, na revista científica Ecology. Além do recorde, os resultados indicam que populações de cães-selvagens separadas por centenas de quilômetros podem estar mais conectadas do que se imaginava.
Os animais pertenciam à matilha Mayukuyuku, no Parque Nacional de Kafue, na Zâmbia. Em julho de 2025, quatro fêmeas de 3 anos deixaram o grupo. Cerca de duas semanas depois, três machos da mesma idade também partiram.
Para acompanhar os deslocamentos, pesquisadores instalaram uma coleira de rastreamento por rádio em um integrante de cada grupo.
Apesar de Kafue oferecer grande quantidade de presas e extensas áreas protegidas, os cães seguiram para regiões cada vez mais distantes. Ao longo da jornada, passaram por áreas com menor proteção e chegaram aos arredores de cidades como Kabwe, Kitwe e Ndola.
Em setembro do ano passado, depois de ambos os grupos percorrerem mais de mil quilômetros desde o território original, machos e fêmeas chegaram a se reencontrar durante um único dia. Depois, voltaram a seguir caminhos diferentes.
Os três machos continuaram para o leste, atravessaram dois grandes reservatórios e finalmente se estabeleceram em uma região próxima à escarpa do Vale do Rift, cerca de 419 quilômetros em linha direta do local onde nasceram. Por causa do trajeto sinuoso, no entanto, eles percorreram 4.126 quilômetros até chegar ao novo território.
Segundo os pesquisadores, trata-se da maior distância de dispersão já registrada para qualquer mamífero africano. Como comparação, os gnus podem percorrer até cerca de 1.800 quilômetros durante a migração anual entre Quênia e Tanzânia.
Os cães-selvagens-africanos (Lycaon pictus) vivem em grupos familiares com uma estrutura social rígida. Normalmente, apenas um casal dominante se reproduz dentro de cada matilha.
Animais subordinados podem permanecer no grupo ajudando a cuidar dos filhotes ou partir em busca de parceiros e de um território onde tenham maior chance de reprodução.
Os sete animais acompanhados tinham 3 anos e poucas perspectivas de se reproduzir permanecendo na matilha Mayukuyuku, segundo os pesquisadores. A espécie também possui características físicas favoráveis a longos deslocamentos, incluindo pernas compridas e grande resistência.
A trajetória das quatro fêmeas teve um desfecho diferente. Em outubro de 2025, dados da coleira mostraram que uma delas começou a realizar movimentos repetidos de ida e volta. Os pesquisadores consideram provável que uma das fêmeas sem coleira tenha ficado presa em uma armadilha de arame usada para caça, enquanto as outras permaneceram próximas.
Dias depois, a própria coleira de rastreamento foi cortada, interrompendo o acompanhamento do grupo. Segundo os pesquisadores, essas armadilhas estão entre as principais ameaças atuais aos cães-selvagens-africanos.
Os animais em dispersão também enfrentam riscos naturais. Leões podem matar adultos e filhotes, hienas disputam suas presas e a travessia de rios pode colocá-los diante de crocodilos.
O percurso também trouxe novas informações sobre a distribuição da espécie. Em determinado momento, os machos passaram a poucos quilômetros de um grupo de fêmeas localizado no leste da Zâmbia, a mais de 500 quilômetros de Kafue.
Para os autores, esse tipo de deslocamento sugere que populações aparentemente isoladas podem manter conexões entre diferentes ecossistemas do leste e do sul da África.
Há também sinais de recolonização de áreas onde os cães-selvagens haviam desaparecido. O Parque Nacional de Kasungu, no Malawi, por exemplo, registrou recentemente a presença da espécie pela primeira vez em mais de uma década.
Ao mesmo tempo, as enormes distâncias percorridas mostram o grau de fragmentação dos habitats. Os pesquisadores destacam, por isso, a importância de preservar corredores ecológicos entre áreas protegidas, permitindo que os animais se desloquem entre diferentes populações.
O cão-selvagem-africano está entre os mamíferos mais ameaçados do continente, e a conservação da espécie depende não apenas de reservas isoladas, mas também da manutenção das áreas utilizadas durante esses longos deslocamentos.

title: Content Creator and Her Grandparents Receive Unexpected Gift: "Something We Never Imagined Having in Cuba"
content:
Young Cuban content creator Lauren Daniela, recognized on Instagram as @laurenlotti_, endured one of the toughest days of the year with her family in Matanzas. They were all battling fevers, their solar panels rendered useless by the rain, and power outages complicating even the preservation of food.
Amidst this turmoil, a gift from Italy arrived like a miracle: an EcoFlow generator sent by a follower. "Nadia, that angel who cares so much for us, sent us this much-needed surprise. A generator," Lauren shared in her reel.
The video starkly depicts what such equipment means in Cuba in 2026. "You can't imagine what it means to have this now in Cuba," Lauren stated, highlighting a detail that underscores the crisis’s depth: "It's incredible that today, if you go to a notary to get an ID card or other paperwork done, you need to bring a generator because it's the only way they can serve you."
“This feels like a dream for us,” Lauren expressed as she showed off the generator beside her grandparents. “We are immensely grateful because our lives have truly changed. And it’s all thanks to every one of you.”
Struggles with Energy in Cuba
The family already owned two solar panels, but on cloudy or rainy days, they were insufficient to power the water pump and keep food from spoiling. The EcoFlow generator—portable power stations with prices ranging from approximately $368 to over $2,600 on the market—is an almost unattainable luxury for many Cubans, equivalent to months or even years of average wages on the island.
The energy context surrounding this video is dire. On September 18, Cuba experienced its eighth total disconnect from the National Electric System, and the power generation deficit has repeatedly exceeded 2,000 MW this month.
Documenting the Reality
For months, Lauren has been documenting this unfiltered reality and channeling donations from her international community into concrete aid. In April, she brought attention to her grandfather's pension—3,727 Cuban pesos, less than eight dollars after 40 years of work—sparking a wave of solidarity.
In July, she achieved what seemed impossible: purchasing a more spacious home for her grandparents in Matanzas, away from the hillside they used to live on. A month later, she touched thousands of hearts on social media when she distributed lunches to vulnerable individuals, funded by her audience primarily from Spain, the United States, Venezuela, and the Dominican Republic.
Understanding Cuba's Energy Crisis
Why is a generator so crucial for families in Cuba?
Due to frequent power outages and the unreliable state of the national electric system, having a generator is often the only way families can ensure a stable electricity supply to preserve food and perform daily tasks.
How have Cubans been coping with the energy shortage?
Many Cubans rely on alternative solutions like solar panels and generators to cope with the energy shortage. However, these solutions are costly and not accessible to everyone, reflecting the severe impact of the ongoing energy crisis.

title: No more book bans: how Florida students are pushing rightwingers out of school boards
content:
Jimmy Glover’s youngest children were in high school when he noticed their Florida school district taking an unsettling turn. Beloved books were being pulled from shelves. Teachers were scared of being targeted.
“There was this culture of fear that was permeating throughout the district,” Glover said of Sarasota county.
By channeling anger against mask mandates in schools, the rightwing group Moms for Liberty, founded in Florida, built an outsized influence on school boards across the country in 2022. Soon, members began pressuring schools to remake their curricula along conservative ideological lines, erasing mentions of LGBTQ+ Americans, slavery, racism and more.
As a Black dad living in a historically Black part of Sarasota, Glover said he was especially disturbed by governor Ron DeSantis’s announcement that Florida schools would begin teaching students that some Black people benefited from slavery. “Now my children and the students in my community weren’t going to be learning about the true history of this country,” Glover said.
So the father of four decided to run for Sarasota’s school board this year. He is part of a larger movement of students, parents, teachers and concerned community members pushing back against the influence of groups like Moms for Liberty in Florida public education. They wanted schools that were safe and welcoming for all students, and that focused on learning rather than scoring points on the national political scene.
And last month, they won.
Progressive candidates beat opponents backed by or aligned with Moms for Liberty in school board races across the state – in many cases reversing gains made by the group in 2022. Of the 30 candidates the group supported that year, 20 have declined to seek re-election, have been defeated or will face runoffs in November, according to the LGBTQ+ rights group Equality Florida.
In Sarasota, home to Moms for Liberty’s cofounder Bridget Ziegler, progressives flipped the school board, with liberal candidates Megan Tennimon and Beth Mayberry replacing more conservative members (school board races in Florida are technically nonpartisan). Glover got more votes than either of his conservative opponents, but his race will go to a runoff in November since no candidate won a majority.
When reached for comment, Moms for Liberty referred the Guardian to a public statement disputing the notion that the recent Florida election represented a loss for the group: “Moms for Liberty-endorsed school board candidates won or advanced in 11 of 15 races across Florida.” But the group had issued fewer endorsements than in past elections and declined to endorse any candidate in several counties. That included Sarasota county, where board chair Ziegler, who has been plagued by scandal, was not running for re-election.
Meanwhile, organizers for Glover’s campaign and others say the elections in Florida mark a turning point, a rejection of rightwing educational ideology in a deep-red part of a deep-red state. And, they say, the victories hold lessons for progressives campaigning on the national stage in the midterms and beyond.
“We know that a better future is possible,” said Sebastian Martinez, president of the Sarasota Next Gen Democrats, a youth organizing group that helped campaign for the county’s progressive slate. “We’ll work every day to get there.”
Students step up and organize
Glover wasn’t the only Florida parent concerned about the influence of Moms for Liberty over his children’s education. The group had success in 2022 by appealing to voters angry about pandemic school closures, and by joining the larger rightwing campaign against “critical race theory”. But Moms for Liberty’s popularity has waned since then, said Liv Coleman, a professor of political science and international studies at the University of Tampa.
By the time Stephanie Vanos ran for Orange county’s school board in 2024, the top question voters asked her was: “Are you the one who wants to ban books?”
“It speaks to the outrage at state censorship in our schools and the complete disrespect for the first amendment,” said Vanos, who won her seat that year.
But that outrage had yet to be fully harnessed.
Martinez, now 22, has been active in school board organizing since he was 16. He started Next Gen Democrats last year as a way to expand young Sarasotans’ role in Democratic politics. “I really wanted to see young people not just get involved in organizing, but to become part of the party,” he said.
For youth, one barrier to political participation is money, Martinez said – they can’t afford to volunteer their time when they could be working a paid job. So to help recruit and retain young canvassers, the group offered $20 an hour. “The Democratic party is supposed to be a party of working-class people supporting working-class people, and so it only makes sense to then pay people to work,” Martinez said.
Sarasota Next Gen Democrats recruited about 20 high school students to phone bank, knock on doors and distribute yard signs around the county, said Kennedy Cole, the group’s political director. They also helped decorate a school bus that drove around Sarasota on Election Day, getting the word out about progressive candidates.
Students “were sick of what we’ve seen from our school board, and we knew that Megan, Beth and Jimmy would help return normalcy to it”, said Cole, a 17-year-old high school senior. “Students really worked their butts off to get those results.”
It wasn’t just students. Youth organizers met regularly with other community activists, including a group of retired women who sent 7,000 handwritten postcards to Sarasota voters. A parents’ group invited candidates to a local park to meet voters while their kids played. Equality Florida spent $250,000 on mailers in support of candidates around the state who were facing opponents aligned with Moms for Liberty.
“In order to do something like this, it takes a web of people,” Cole said. “It’s a lot of different people operating in their own ways.”
‘Tired of the chaos’
Whether they were knocking on doors or meeting families at the playground, winning candidates spread a back-to-basics message that resonated with voters across political lines. Cole likes to tell the story of a close friend whose conservative parents voted for liberal school board candidates “because they were tired of the chaos” that Moms for Liberty had brought.
Sarasota schools’ statewide ranking had slipped since conservative activists took control of the school board, said Mayberry, a former teacher who won a seat representing Sarasota’s fifth district. “The focus came off of academic performance,” Mayberry said.
She and other successful candidates campaigned to restore that focus. They ran on issues like school funding, academic achievement and support for teachers and students, Coleman said. “They really just focused on things that affected people’s everyday lives.”
That approach could be instructive for candidates around the country, in November and beyond. Sarasota Next Gen Democrats and their allies built a movement that was “not right v left, not parents v students, not students v teachers”, Cole said. “We were able to organize as a community coalition of people who were sick and tired of political games being played with our students and our education, and want a better change for the future.”
That future includes continuing to campaign for Glover, who will face Republican-backed candidate Heidi Brandt in a runoff election in November. If Glover wins, he would be the first person of color ever to serve on the Sarasota county school board. He’ll also have his work cut out for him in a district reeling from book ban battles and facing funding cuts as a statewide school voucher program pulls money from public schools.
“We have a big challenge coming up,” he said. “We’re coming out of a time when culture wars and personal agendas dominated the headlines, so we have a lot of work to do.”
But he and the organizers behind him are optimistic – not just about Sarasota, but about the country as a whole.
“If it can happen here,” Martinez said of the victories this August, “it can happen anywhere.”

title: Abu Dhabi Digital Skills Card: What it is, who can get it and how to apply in 2026
content: Dubai: Abu Dhabi is making professional credentials easier to verify, thanks to the newly introduced Digital Skills Card.What is this card and how do you acquire it? Find out below.What is the Digital Skills Card?Last week, the UAE saw the launch of the Gulf region’s first Digital Skills Card.It was introduced by the Abu Dhabi Quality and Conformity Council (QCC), an Abu Dhabi government entity that leads and improves efficiency in quality standards, conformity, and measurement systems across industries, in partnership with Union Assessment and Quality Accreditation (UAC), an organisation that tests and certifies the job skills of workers in collaboration with the Abu Dhabi government.The Digital Skills Card provides a secure, digitally verifiable record of an individual’s professional skills and qualifications, making it easier for employers, regulators and government entities to corroborate this information. How does it work?The initiative uses cutting-edge blockchain technology to verify workforce credentials.According to the QCC, each card is linked to a certification that has been awarded through personnel conformity programmes that are accredited by QCC and delivered by the UAC.When required, employers or other authorities can scan the card’s QR code to verify the certification’s validity and authenticity.Why the need for a Digital Skills Card?The Digital Skills Card has several benefits, according to UAC:It ensures a quick, convenient way to confirm a professional’s credentials.It improves transparency.It removes the need for paper certificates through digitisation.It ensures verified skills travel with the individual, improving workforce mobility across the GCC.The skills are recognised across institutions and borders.Workforce credentials retain their value wherever the professional’s career takes them, regardless of time passed.Although it was launched just last week, the UAC expects to expand the scope of the Digital Skills Card, and add a broader range of certifications, qualifications, and professional achievements.Who can get a Digital Skills Card?The Digital Skills Card is for certified professionals from diverse industry backgrounds, who have completed accredited personnel conformity programmes.Some examples include workers in regulated sectors, such as oil and gas, electrical services, building, school transport, and public health.What are personnel conformity programmes?The Abu Dhabi QCC manages personnel conformity programmes in the emirate, with the aim of certifying that individuals who offer professional services meet mandatory emirate and industry standards.The QCC provides conformity programme services in four main fields: products, personnel, production systems and administrative. For the Digital Skills Card, you are required to undergo a personnel conformity programme – the QCC will assess you to ensure your competencies, abilities and skills meet the emirate’s standards required to practice your occupation or profession.A Personnel Conformity Certificate is granted to individuals who pass the necessary tests, according to the conformity programme for their occupation or craft. This is reflected in your Digital Skills Card, and is made visible to any regulators or employers who access it via your QR code.How do I access personnel conformity programmes?Follow these four steps to receive a Personnel Conformity Certificate:Visit Abu Dhabi QCC’s website – qcc.gov.ae – and log in with your UAE PASS.Select ‘E-Services’. Choose a service, based on your industry. For instance, if you are an electrical engineer, you could choose ‘Issue certificate of conformity for personnel working in electrical professions’. In this section, you can also review the expectations for your upcoming assessment, as well as fees based on your specific profession.Select a designated assessment centre, and select the time and date of your assessment.Arrive at the assessment centre on the appointed date with the following required documents, as well as any others mentioned on the QCC website for your specific profession:Valid passportValid Emirates IDYour Bachelor’s degree or diploma in your chosen profession, or equivalency certificateExperience certificate in the same fieldPay the fees.Complete the assessment.The QCC will review your assessment and documents, and if approved, you will receive a certificate of conformity, which affirms that the certificate-holder has fulfilled the relevant professional standards approved by the regulatory bodies in the emirate to practice their profession or craft.Fees: Fees differ based on your industry, but range from Dh650 to Dh1,500.Once you earn your certification, the results will be updated on your Digital Skills Card and you will receive it electronically, along with a QR code.
